## 中文

用**华为云 OAuth 登录**，在 OpenCode 和 magpie 里提供两个供应商：

- **华为云码道（CodeArts Agent）**的编码套餐（体验版、个人与企业积分套餐），模型为 GLM、DeepSeek、
  openPangu 等。provider id：`codearts`。
- **OfficeAce（华为云 AgentArts / MaaS）**：GLM、DeepSeek、Qwen、Kimi、盘古等模型，分桶积分与每日签到。
  provider id：`officeace`。

两张卡各自登录：两个 provider 各持一条记录、各有一个华为云 refresh token —— STS 的 refresh token 只能用一次，
两条记录共用一个 token 会互相把对方注销。同一个华为云 IAM 账号对两家都有效，且一次登录换到的凭据对两家的接口都能用
（已实测，见下），所以「登两次」只是多点一次，不会有别的不便。OfficeAce 在 0.3.0 之前是独立的 `officeace-auth` 包：
那些账号按 magpie 原有的位置与形状读取，**不用重新登录**。

> **非官方插件**：与华为、华为云及 CodeArts（码道）没有任何关联，也未获其授权或认可。插件调用的是
> 码道客户端使用的非公开接口，并以与官方客户端相同的方式标识自己（含自动领取每日免费权益与签到），
> 这可能不符合华为云的服务条款，接口也可能随时变更。使用风险（包括账号受限）由使用者自行承担。

- **登录**：华为云 OAuth（PKCE + DPoP），本机 `127.0.0.1`（端口 ≥ 10000）接收回调，向 STS 换取临时
  AK/SK/security-token；回调只接受精确的 `/oauth/callback` GET，回调不带 code（portal 报错）时立即判定登录失败。完整凭据（含 refresh_token、PKCE verifier、DPoP 私钥）以 JSON 存在账号的
  `access` 字段里，保存在 magpie / OpenCode 自己的账号存储中；过期前 30 分钟自动续期，请求遇到临时凭据
  过期时就地续期并重发一次。同一账号的 refresh_token 只用一次；续期只是暂时失败（如 STS 连不上）时返回
  `503` 并保留登录，只有被 STS 明确拒绝才标记需要重新登录。账号标识取自 refresh_token，重复登录不会多出账号。
- **模型**：账号实时的内置模型列表；领取当日免费权益成功后，再加上免费模型（每个北京自然日领一次，与
  客户端一致；当天还没领取时遇到 `benefit not found` 也会先领取再重发）。每个模型的「消耗系数」作为 magpie 的倍率上报，来自账号主智能体（`build`）的模型列表。
- **请求**：SDK-HMAC-SHA256 签名，只签给码道自己的两个主机（`snap-access.cn-north-4.myhuaweicloud.com`、
  `opengw.developer.huaweicloud.com`），发往其他地址（如改过的 `api`）的请求在凭据发出前就被拒绝，签名请求和令牌请求都不跟随重定向；像客户端一样发送 `x-ot-session-id` 会话头（每账号一个会话），账号内
  在途请求不超过 3 个，`TM.00001041` 退避重试，网关排队时按客户端的方式等待（0.2.3 起，magpie 在这个请求之后还有别的账号、供应商或路由组成员时（`x-magpie-fallback: 1`），排队的请求立即退出队列并以 `503` 加队列的 `Retry-After` 回答，magpie 随即改问下一个）；总是以流式请求上游（码道
  只对流式回答计量积分），调用方要非流式时折叠回 JSON；默认注入 `thinking: { type: "enabled" }`，思考与
  正文分开；200 里内嵌的错误换算为 `429` / `400` / `502` 并带厂商原话；码道只接受不超过 64 个字符的工具名，
  更长的（如 MCP 工具名）发出时缩为前 55 个字符 + `_` + 8 位 SHA-256，回答（流式与非流式）里的工具调用再换回原名。
  0.2.4 起所有模型都声明为只收文本（码道对图片回 `InferHub.001001020.406`「The request model is not multimodal」），
  magpie 会替模型描述图片或把图片略去；这个拒绝不论放在 200 里还是带别的状态码，都换算为 `400`，而不是让智能体反复重试的 `502`。
- **用量与签到**：总积分决定账号是否可用，其余积分桶只做明细；另有每日免费额度窗口。各批积分的到期
  时间读自码道控制台同一批接口，读不到时退回插件的签到账本 `~/.config/magpie/codearts-checkins.json`
  （这部分仍在用更多账号验证，请以控制台为准）。`auth.checkin` 与客户端「限时福利 → 每日领取」一致
  （插件领取后确认失败的，当天记在签到账本里，下次签到时补确认；客户端本就不确认的 `id: null` 领取不会被确认），
  在 **设置 → 用量 → Plugins** 打开「每日自动签到」即可。
- **OfficeAce（第二个供应商）**：officeace 卡片提供与 CodeArts 卡片相同的「华为云登录」，账号体系是同一套：
  码道的 STS 三元组能签 OfficeAce 的订阅接口（V11-HMAC）并通过它的 CLAW 权限校验，反之 OfficeAce 的三元组也能签
  码道的 `snap-access` 接口。但**两张卡各写各的记录、各持自己的 refresh token**——一次登录只写当前这张卡的记录。
  华为云的 refresh token 只能用一次，两条记录共用一个 token 会让 CodeArts 用户因为 OfficeAce 那条记录续期而被要求
  重新登录；一条记录一次登录才是对的。要用 OfficeAce 就在 OfficeAce 卡片上登录。记录放在
  `<provider>#<账号身份哈希>` 上，之后再登同一账号会合并，不会多出一行。**只有登录会创建 OfficeAce 账号**：
  列模型时不会从另一家的记录「带入」一个账号，用户登出的账号不会自己回来。老 `officeace-auth` 的记录原样读取：provider id 相同、`access` 里的 JSON 形状相同，
  续期仍走它签发时的 OAuth 客户端（`pdp5_for_agentarts`）。
- **账号名与续期边界**：`accountId` 用厂商自己的稳定 id（IAM 域名 id，与老 `officeace-auth` 记录里的一致），
  **绝不是打码手机号**（#483、magpie#4416；magpie 把用户给账号起的名字、代理、网关 key 都挂在 `accountId` 上，
  手机号只出现在 `usage().user`）。续期不会重命名账号：记录里已有的 `accountId`/`uid` 原样保留（域名 id，或
  `officeace-auth` 0.1.14 存下的手机号），只在该值为空时才补一个。新登录写的 `accountId` 是域名 id。
  续期只花**这条记录自己的 refresh token**：协调单位是「refresh chain = 签发它的 OAuth 客户端 + token 的血缘」
  （轮换后的新 token 记在父 token 同一血缘上，仍算同一条链）。
  每条记录都有自己的 token：码道记录由 `codearts-agent` 签发，OfficeAce 记录由 `pdp5_for_agentarts` 签发，各花各的，
  各自保留自己的 MaaS 凭据；**续期只写被续的那条记录，绝不写另一条**（`auth.set` 会把不存在的账号创建出来），
  续期失败就是失败，绝不借用另一条链的凭据。
- **OfficeAce 的模型**：目录 `/v2/models` 是注册表（26 条，多数对话时回 `404 ModelArts.81009 Invalid model`），
  插件只保留计费清单（`/v1/model-token-rates`，9 条）里的，并永不列出三个实测必 404 的 id；倍率表读取失败时保留上
  一份好表（空表会让不可调的 id 全部回到用户面前）；未登录时用 10 个内置模型兜底。模型名带上倍率（`GLM-5.3 · x0.18`），
  上游 `model_name` 的尾部换行会去掉。
- **OfficeAce 的请求**：MaaS 要 `Authorization: Basic base64(appKey:appSecret)`，插件把 SDK 的 Bearer 改写掉，
  去掉 `officeace/` 前缀，发到凭据里自带的 MaaS 地址（为空时用官方直连）。`401`（或 4xx 但报文点名这对 Basic 凭据）
  会先续期一次再重发，**但只有续期真的换了这对凭据时才重发**。已登录但没开通 MaaS 的账号会得到一条说清原因的 `400`，
  不会把空的 Basic 头发给上游。
- **OfficeAce 的用量与签到**：`/v1/subscription` 的套餐桶（`skus[].quotas`）与活动桶（`bonus_skus`）转成 magpie 的窗口；
  `.trial` 桶没有到期时间就不显示；已过期的桶收进折叠区（`aside`）且不参与路由。签到是每个北京自然日一次
  `POST /v1/subscription/bonus/claim`：2xx 但 `bonus_skus` 为空是「今日已无新增可领」（`done`），不是失败。
- **已知限制**：STS 的 refresh_token 只能用一次。本包的每张卡各自登录、各自持有一条记录与一个 token，所以两张卡
  互不影响；**续期只写被续的那条记录**，因此用户删掉的账号永远不会被写回来（无论它此前有没有被列出/使用过、
  有没有重启）。老 `officeace-auth` 记录同样只按自己的链续期。两个 magpie 进程同时续期同一个账号仍可能撞车，
  输的一方重试，只有 token 一直是被消费状态才标记需重新登录。
  另外，`officeace-auth` 与本包不能同时服务 `officeace` 这个 provider id，magpie 会让你选一个，装之前先卸掉旧的。
- **致谢**：原作者 [yuweihao17](https://github.com/yuweihao17/codearts)；HuHong-Tao、ReachForStar 的
  实测与实现；[Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model](https://github.com/Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model)。

@magpie-community/opencode-commandcode-a.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-commandcode-auth

Signs in to a [Command Code](https://commandcode.ai) plan (Pro, GOAT, Max,
Ultra, Go, Teams Pro) and makes its requests, in OpenCode and in magpie.
Provider id: `commandcode-plan`.

## Signing in

An account is a Command Code API key. There are three ways to get one:

- **Command Code (browser)**: the CLI's own sign-in. Studio asks you to
  approve a key for this machine, then posts it to a callback on
  `127.0.0.1`. The plugin checks the key with `/alpha/whoami` and reads the
  plan.
- **Command Code CLI's sign-in**: takes the account `commandcode login`
  signed in to, from `~/.commandcode/auth.json`. The file is only read,
  never changed.
- **API key**: paste a key from
  [commandcode.ai/settings/keys](https://commandcode.ai/settings/keys).

The key is kept where OpenCode keeps sign-ins (`auth.json`; in magpie,
`plugin-auth.json`) as `{ "type": "api", "key", "metadata": { "email": <user>, "plan" } }`.
Keys don't expire, so there is nothing to refresh. A key Command Code
turns away (revoked, or signed out in Studio) marks the account signed out
in magpie, which passes over it and offers Sign in again on its row: a
usage read, or a request answered 401, asks `/alpha/whoami`, and when that
refuses the key too, says `signIn: "expired"` (`X-Magpie-Sign-In: expired`
on the request's answer). A clean usage read takes the mark off.

## Requests

- **Every plan but Go** uses the Provider API at
  `https://api.commandcode.ai/provider/v1`. Every request carries the key
  as both `Authorization: Bearer` and `x-api-key`.
  - Claude models speak Anthropic's Messages API.
  - The other models speak chat completions.
- **Go** has no Provider API access. Its key is only accepted where the CLI
  asks, `POST /alpha/generate`, in the CLI's own format (command-code
  1.72.2 and its headers). The plugin's `fetch` handles this:
  - It turns OpenCode's chat completion into that format.
  - It turns the line-by-line reply back into a chat completion, streamed
    or not.
  - Failures keep their statuses: a model the plan lacks is a 403, running
    out of credits is a 402, and a usage-window limit is a 429.
  - A reply that stops before its finish line is a 502, unless it was
    streamed and had already said something. Then it ends cut short, with
    a note saying so, and `[DONE]` (#91).

The plan is read from `/alpha/billing/subscriptions`. It is cached for 10
minutes; after a failed read, the plugin tries again after 1 minute.
When the plan isn't known yet and the Provider API refuses the key with
"Your Go plan doesn't include API access", the key is taken as Go's from
then on (and saved so with it), and a chat completion is sent again to
`/alpha/generate`.

## Zero Data Retention

[Zero Data Retention](https://commandcode.ai/docs/resources/zdr) sends
requests only to upstreams that keep no prompts or replies. It is off
until you turn it on, either way:

- **In magpie**: turn on **Zero Data Retention** in the Command Code
  provider's editor (magpie v0.1.1231 or later). The switch is read at
  each request, so it needs no restart.
- **Anywhere** (OpenCode too): set `CMD_ZDR=1` in the environment of the
  process the plugin runs in, as for Command Code's CLI. Only `1` turns it
  on.

While it is on, every request for a reply carries `x-cmd-zdr: 1`, on the
Provider API and on Go's `/alpha/generate` alike, as the CLI sends it with `CMD_ZDR=1`.
ZDR requests usually cost more. A model with no ZDR upstream is refused,
and the refusal reaches the agent as Command Code said it: on the Provider
API a 422 with code `cmd_zdr_no_providers`, on Go a 400 whose type is
`cmd_zdr_no_providers`. Turn the switch off, or pick another model.

## Models

The `config` hook declares the default list:

| Model | Context window |
|---|---|
| Claude Sonnet 5 | 1M |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 1M |
| GPT-6 Sol | 1.05M |
| DeepSeek V4 Pro | 1M |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 1M |
| Kimi K3 | 1M |
| GLM-5.3 | 1M |
| MiniMax M3 | 1M |

Once signed in, the `provider.models` hook replaces the default list with
the account's own:

Command Code's `/models` list is the same for every plan. A plan's list is
that list less the models the plan may not use, as the CLI's own table
(command-code 1.79.2) has it:

- **Go** and **GOAT** may not use the premium models (Claude Sonnet 5 and
  Opus, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, …). Go is also blocked from GOAT's own
  (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Grok 4.6 and 4.7, …).
- **Pro** may not use Claude Opus and Fable, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and
  Fugu Ultra; **Provider** may not use GPT-6.1 Sol.
- **Max**, **Ultra** and **Teams Pro** may use every model.

An account with bought or free credits may use every model, and so may one
whose plan can't be read: then the whole list is shown. A model the plan
doesn't have is still refused by Command Code (403 `MODEL_NOT_IN_PLAN`), and
that refusal reaches the agent.

- **Every plan but Go**: the Provider API's `/models` list. Each model's
  `supported_endpoints` picks the API it speaks.
- **Go**: the same `/models` list, asked without the key (it answers
  without one, and Go's key has no Provider API). That is 56 models as of
  2026-10-13. When the list can't be had, the CLI's own Go table (57
  models) stands in.

  The Go models carry their reasoning levels, and a requested level is
  fitted to the nearest one the model has.

Thinking can be turned off on the Provider API for DeepSeek V4 Pro, V4
Flash, V4 Flash Vision (exp), V4.1 Flash and V4.1 Flash Fast. These models
offer an off level (`none`), and the plugin sends it as Command Code's
`reasoning_effort: "off"`. A client's own `"off"` is sent the same way. The
other models, DeepSeek V4 Flash Fast and Kimi K3 among them, refuse `"off"`,
so turning thinking off sends them no level. Go's `/alpha/generate` hasn't
been tried with `"off"`, so it is sent no level there either.

The `/models` list doesn't say which models take images. A model is marked
as taking them when it is a Claude model, or when the default list or the
CLI's table says so. For any other model the plugin says nothing either
way, and magpie answers from models.dev, as its built-in did.

## Jev, a decision model

Command Code serves TypeSafe's Jev (`typesafe/jev`), a decision model: it
answers typed questions (`{"state", "questions"}`) with probabilities, and
holds no conversation. Its `/models` list doesn't name it, so the plugin
adds it to every plan's list, marked `decides`, and sets `decide` on the
provider. magpie then offers it as a routing group's classifier and at its
`/v1/systemone` (as `commandcode-plan/typesafe/jev`), never to an agent to
chat with. A question goes to `POST /provider/v1/systemone` as the CLI
(1.88.2) sends it, with the CLI's headers, and Zero Data Retention when the
switch is on. Command Code decides which plans may use it; a refusal reaches
magpie with its status, as a chat's does.

## Not included

- Usage and quota (`/alpha/billing/credits`, the 5-hour and weekly windows).
- Switching between several accounts. OpenCode keeps one sign-in per
  provider.

@magpie-community/opencode-copilot-auth.readme:
# GitHub Copilot

An unofficial OpenCode provider plugin for GitHub Copilot on GitHub.com and
GitHub Enterprise (including GHE.com). In magpie it also shows the account's
premium request or credit quota: used, remaining, the included allowance and
when it resets. It does not change the subscription or enable paid overage.

The authentication and request implementation is adapted from
[`opencode-copilot-auth` 0.0.12](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-copilot-auth)
([source](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode-copilot-auth)), under its MIT
license, retained in `LICENSE`. It keeps the device flow, request signing,
initiator detection and vision headers, with client versions matching magpie's
native Copilot implementation. No runtime dependency on another installed plugin
or local file is needed.

## Install and sign in

```sh
magpie plugin add @magpie-community/opencode-copilot-auth
magpie plugin login github-copilot
```

Choose GitHub.com or GitHub Enterprise; for Enterprise enter your own GitHub
host, such as `company.ghe.com`. Complete GitHub's device authorization in
the browser. Host inputs must be HTTPS origins without credentials, paths,
query strings or custom ports. As in the upstream plugin, Enterprise API and
inference hosts are `api.<host>` and `copilot-api.<host>`; deployments with
different endpoint layouts are not covered.

For OpenCode, add `@magpie-community/opencode-copilot-auth` to `plugin` in
`opencode.json`, then run `opencode auth login`.

The provider id is `github-copilot` for both deployments. GitHub's OAuth token
is stored in the host's auth store as `refresh`; the short-lived Copilot token
is stored as `access` with `expires`. In magpie this is `plugin-auth.json`,
scoped by the host to the selected account, including additional `#slot`
accounts. Enterprise sign-ins keep `enterpriseUrl` through token renewal.
Models come from the host's existing `github-copilot` catalog.

If the original `opencode-copilot-auth` is already installed in magpie, keep
it and explicitly choose which plugin serves the existing provider:

```sh
magpie plugin use @magpie-community/opencode-copilot-auth github-copilot
```

The shared provider id lets the new plugin reuse the existing sign-in and
model picks; there is no automatic migration from magpie's separate built-in
`copilot` provider or from a legacy `github-copilot-enterprise` auth entry.

## Quota reporting

magpie calls `auth.usage(getAuth, provider)` independently of model requests.
It reads `GET /copilot_internal/user` on `api.github.com` or the account's
`api.<enterpriseUrl>` using the GitHub OAuth token, **not** the short-lived
inference token. Reading quota neither renews nor persists either token.
OpenCode ignores magpie's additional hook.

- Only `chat`, `completions` and `premium_interactions` snapshots are read;
  unknown quota types cannot block chat model routing.
- Snapshot counters accept numbers or numeric strings. Fractional
  `quota_remaining` takes precedence over the rounded legacy `remaining`;
  `remaining` is the fallback when the canonical field is absent. Used amount
  is entitlement minus remaining. Organization-pool `credits_used` has no
  per-seat denominator and is never divided by entitlement. Without remaining
  counters or a percentage, a finite seat's utilization is unknown.
- Snapshot amounts determine the percentage when known; otherwise
  `percent_remaining` gives a percentage without inventing an absolute balance.
- `quota_reset_at`, `quota_reset_date_utc` and `quota_reset_date` supply resets;
  date-only values mean UTC midnight. Legacy free-plan monthly counters are
  supported too.
- `has_quota: false` does not hide a usable or exhausted seat. A zero
  entitlement means no included allowance. An exhausted premium pool may say
  `unlimited: true, has_quota: false`; it is shown as 100% used, not unlimited.
- Unlimited chat and completion allowances are labelled `Unlimited`, not
  `0 / 0`. An unlimited premium credit pool with readable `credits_used` shows
  that usage as informational (`aside`), without inventing a seat limit or
  percentage. Completion quotas do not block chat model routing. For finite
  premium allowances, only unmanaged seats with vendor-permitted overage are
  informational (`aside`); Business and Enterprise exhaustion remains blocking,
  as in magpie's native Copilot implementation. The plugin never changes the
  overage permission or adds the separate overage counter to included usage.
- Empty, malformed or unavailable quota data is unknown, not zero usage.
  Only an explicit HTTP 401 marks the sign-in expired. Network errors, rate
  limits, 403s and server errors keep the sign-in. No response body or token is
  included in error messages. Quota requests have a timeout and reject redirects.

GitHub's quota endpoint is internal and may change. An organization may not
expose all balances to a seat; missing data is not an estimate of its budget.

## Network and credential scope

The new network operation is a read of `GET /copilot_internal/user`. It sends
the account's GitHub OAuth token only to `https://api.github.com` or, for an
Enterprise sign-in, `https://api.<enterpriseUrl>`. Enter only the GitHub host
your organization trusts: HTTPS validation does not establish ownership of a
domain. The quota request rejects redirects, and sends no prompt, model
request, local file or inference token.

The inherited device flow posts the public OAuth client id and device code
to the selected GitHub host's `/login/device/code` and
`/login/oauth/access_token`. Inference token renewal sends the OAuth token to
`/copilot_internal/v2/token` on that account's API host. Model requests use
the Copilot inference token at `https://api.githubcopilot.com` or the
Enterprise `https://copilot-api.<enterpriseUrl>` origin. These operations are
separate from reading quota.

The plugin gets credentials from the host's `getAuth`; it does not scan
credential files, a keychain or agent configurations. Only the existing
inference token renewal calls `client.auth.set`. No dependency, install
script, telemetry, relay or account migration is added.

Request signing preserves host headers (including `Content-Type`, `Accept` and
`chat.headers`) supplied as a `Headers` object, plain object or tuples. It replaces
authorization and removes `x-api-key` case-insensitively. If the host stops
returning OAuth credentials, requests pass through without Copilot signing.

## Tests

```sh
(
  verification_home=$(mktemp -d) || exit
  trap 'rm -rf "$verification_home"' EXIT
  HOME="$verification_home" bun test packages/copilot
)
bun scripts/check.mjs copilot
```

Tests use synthetic accounts, mocked vendor responses and a loopback HTTP server:
public and Enterprise device flows, token refresh, outgoing request headers and
body, non-OAuth passthrough, fractional credits, legacy requests, unlimited
allowances, organization-pool credits, resets, unknown quota types and read failures.
They read no real auth files and consume no Copilot allowance.
The quota read test also uses an expired inference token and asserts the exact
single OAuth quota request, no auth persistence and unchanged input credentials.
Live inference and Enterprise access require separate verification against a
real account; these offline tests are not evidence of vendor acceptance.

@magpie-community/opencode-cursor-auth.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-cursor-auth

Signs in to a [Cursor](https://cursor.com) subscription (Pro, Pro+, Ultra,
Teams) and makes its requests on the API `cursor-agent` talks to, in
OpenCode and in magpie. Provider id: `cursor`.

## Signing in

An account is a Cursor access token. There are three ways to get one:

- **Cursor (browser)**: the sign-in `cursor-agent login` does. The page
  `cursor.com/loginDeepControl` is opened with a PKCE challenge, and the
  plugin polls `api2.cursor.sh/auth/poll` until the browser has signed in.
  The account is named by its email (`DashboardService/GetMe`).
- **cursor-agent's sign-in**: takes the account `cursor-agent login`
  signed in to. Its token is read from where the CLI keeps it: the macOS
  keychain (`cursor-access-token`), else its `auth.json` (`~/.cursor/`,
  `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cursor/` or `%APPDATA%\Cursor\`). A keychain read is
  kept for 10 seconds, and one the keychain refused (the user said no to
  its dialog) is not asked again for 10 minutes; signing in reads it
  afresh. The plugin never writes it; when it has less than 5 minutes
  left, `cursor-agent status` is run, which renews it.
- **Cursor API key**: a key from cursor.com/dashboard → Integrations. It is
  exchanged for a token at `/auth/exchange_user_api_key`, as the CLI does
  with `CURSOR_API_KEY`, and exchanged again when the token runs out.

Sign-ins are kept where OpenCode keeps them (`auth.json`; in magpie,
`plugin-auth.json`). A browser sign-in's token lasts about two months.
Cursor gives the CLI no way to renew it, so after that you sign in again.

## Requests

OpenCode speaks chat completions (`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`); the
plugin's `fetch` answers them on Cursor's agent API:

- The agent API is the one `ServerConfigService/GetServerConfig` names for
  the account (a team may be served in one region only), else
  `agentn.global.api5.cursor.sh`. A refusal that names a region is tried
  once more with the config asked again.
- A fresh request opens `agent.v1.AgentService/Run`, a Connect stream both
  ways over HTTP/2, with the CLI's headers (`x-cursor-client-type: cli`,
  its version, privacy mode on).
- Where HTTP/2 can't open a Run (an error before its response, or none in
  15 s: a proxy or network that blocks HTTP/2), it goes as Cursor's clients
  run it without HTTP/2: `agent.v1.AgentService/RunSSE` down and a
  `aiserver.v1.BidiService/BidiAppend` for each client message up, over
  HTTP/1.1 on `api2.cursor.sh`, through the proxy magpie gives the request.
  When the failure says HTTP/2 itself can't be had (no head in 15 s,
  "h2 is not supported", no HTTP/2 in ALPN, a protocol error), the Runs
  after it go straight to HTTP/1.1 for 10 minutes; a failed connection
  (refused, no network) or a stream the server refused leaves the next Run
  to try HTTP/2 again. A region error over HTTP/1.1 sends the Run back to
  HTTP/2 at the region's agent host. BidiAppends go up numbered in order,
  up to 16 at a time as cursor-agent sends them. A native session's Run
  sends only its KV replies (the history's blobs) that way; a tool result
  or anything else waits for the appends before it, goes alone, and is
  written once Cursor answered it, so it is never uncertain. A BidiAppend
  with no answer in 60 s (more for a large one) ends the Run, as
  cursor-agent does.
- A new Run imports the whole conversation as AI SDK messages kept as blobs
  the server asks for. The caller's tools are MCP tools, listed in the
  system prompt; the model calls them through Cursor's `CallDynamicTool`,
  and the calls come back as chat completion tool calls. Cursor's own tools
  (shell, file reads, edits) are never run.
- A conversation's Runs share one `conversation_id`, so Cursor sends them
  to the machine that has the prompt cached (Grok on Cursor caches by
  machine). It is made from what names the session — the request's
  `prompt_cache_key` (Codex's thread id), else the session the
  `chat.headers` hook is told — and the conversation's first user message,
  so subagents under one session are conversations of their own. With
  nothing naming the session, each Run has a new one.
- Text, thinking (`reasoning_content`) and token usage come back streamed
  or not. Replayed assistant `reasoning_content` (or `reasoning`) is kept as
  AI SDK reasoning parts in the next Run's transcript, including when a
  caller splits parallel tool calls across assistant messages. It stays
  separate from reply text; no thinking signature is invented.
  Cursor's `input_tokens` counts the cached prompt too: the cache
  read and written is taken out of it, and given as `cached_tokens` and
  `cache_write_tokens`, so it is counted once; its reasoning tokens are
  `reasoning_tokens`. A step that calls tools gets no usage in its Run
  (Cursor tells it only once the tools' results come back in the same
  Run), so once the Run is closed its usage is read from the dashboard's
  usage events, by the Run's conversation id: it shows in about 2.5 s,
  and is looked for up to 6 s. Far from Cursor it shows later than that
  (yetone/magpie#1053), so the step says 0 used and the conversation owes
  it: its next steps collect the event in the background, and a step
  that ends the turn waits for what is still owed, so the conversation
  adds up to what Cursor counted. What a step collected of earlier steps
  is not added to its own count, which a client reads as how full its
  context is: it is `usage.magpie_deferred` (`prompt_tokens`,
  `completion_tokens`, `cached_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens`), which
  magpie bills with the step and clients ignore. An account
  whose events miss the wait 3 steps in a row stops waiting for them.
  With nothing naming the session (so no later step to collect it), or
  an account that can't read its usage events, the step is estimated as
  before.
  Failures keep their statuses: 401 to sign in again, 429 at the
  usage limit, 400 for a prompt too long, 403 for a region refusal.

Tool results can continue a retained Run in the same plugin process. The owner
uses the same session/cache key and first user message as `conversation_id`, so
Task subagents sharing their parent's session can run independently. Retention
waits at most 120 seconds for a result batch and 15 minutes for a Run's total
lifetime. A continuation arriving in the last minute of that lifetime rebuilds
from supplied history before submitting results to the old Run. The absolute
deadline still applies to an active segment; it is never extended by activity.
The pool holds at most 8 owners per account and 32 per process, with
bounded history, blobs, arguments, and pending writes. When pending writes
reach their bound (a long history asks for its blobs at once, and a slow link
drains them slowly), the Run waits for the link to drain, and fails only if it
doesn't for 30 seconds.

A step's calls must all arrive within 30 seconds of each other: Cursor sends
each one once the model has written it, so a step of many long calls can take
longer than that in all (#155).

A Run Cursor stops answering ends with a 502 that says so, retained or
stateless: 60 seconds with no message at all, or 4 minutes with only
Cursor's heartbeats (yetone/magpie#2672, where a Run sent some thinking and
then nothing, and the reply waited until the agent gave up after 5 minutes).
Only time spent waiting on Cursor counts: a retained Run waiting for the
caller's tool results is bounded by the 120 seconds above instead.

Cursor's count of a step's tool calls includes calls the plugin answers itself:
a tool the request doesn't have is refused to the model, and Cursor's own
`get_mcp_tools` is answered with the request's tools. It also includes calls
Cursor completes by itself, which it writes and completes in the step but never
starts on the client or sends to it; those count toward it too. Once the count
has come, a checkpoint whose state waits on exactly the calls the caller was
given also ends the step (#550). The step's calls are the rest.

These are retention limits. A missing, expired, restarted, busy, incompatible,
or full owner uses the original history reconstruction and stateless decoder
on a new Run. Pending parent calls and new input can take that path without
cancelling the parent's owner. Already supplied client tool results become
history; the plugin never executes those external tools. A failed native result
write is reported to that request because its outcome may be uncertain. A later
request can rebuild from its supplied history without submitting the result to
the old native exec again.

A native tool handoff reports zero usage with `magpie_native.accounting=pending`;
the final native answer bills the turn's totals. Its own `prompt_tokens` and
`completion_tokens` are its last model call's share (the larger of that
call's prompt estimate and the turn's mean per call), since a client reads
them as how full its context is; the earlier calls' share is
`usage.magpie_deferred` (#156). An identical completed retry
replays the saved response with zero usage. A native final also collects earlier
stateless debt as `usage.magpie_deferred`, separately from its own prompt total.
If a started native Run is abandoned after a pending handoff, its dashboard
count is owed once to the same account and conversation. Successful final
snapshots, including explicit zero, and cached replays do not enroll that debt.

Dashboard attribution uses event timestamps, rather than when events arrive.
Older debt is bounded strictly before the native Run's start, and keeps that
bound across later stateless Runs so an authoritative native event is not
billed again. An earlier event stamped on or after that boundary cannot be
identified reliably and stays unknown. Missing or ambiguous debt expires after
10 minutes; at most 64 distinct bounded debt groups are kept per account and
conversation, dropping the oldest on overflow. These counts are never guessed
as prior usage. Stateless Runs otherwise keep the dashboard accounting above.
`X-Magpie-Cursor-Continuity` identifies `same-run` or `stateless`, with the fallback
reason where available. A missing native batch count can retry stateless once
before any output is exposed or native result submitted; progressive output is
kept and its later errors are surfaced. A step's declared tool batch waits 30
seconds from Cursor's latest call, count, text or heartbeat, so one long call
written under heartbeats is not cut off; the failure says how many of the
declared calls came.

The existing request builder and model selection remain in use, including the
legacy `thinking=false` mapping for explicit `none`/`off`. Retention adds no
request-field whitelist or strict generation-option validation. Native tool
results preserve ordered text and data-URL images and explicit error flags;
unsupported native result shapes use the legacy history path.

## Models

The `config` hook declares `auto` (Cursor's pick). Once signed in, the
`provider.models` hook lists the account's models from Cursor's model
picker (`AiService/AvailableModels`, as the CLI asks for it, cached 10
minutes), the way pi-cursor-sdk lists Cursor's catalog:

- A model with a `context` parameter is listed once per size, as
  `<model>@<size>` named `<name> @ <size>` (`claude-opus-5-5@300k`,
  "Claude Opus 5.5 @ 300k"), its window that many tokens. A model with none
  is listed once, its window Cursor's `contextTokenLimit` (Max Mode's for a
  model served only in Max Mode); 200K when Cursor gives none.
- Effort is not a model of its own: the model's efforts are its variants,
  and the request's `reasoning_effort` (fitted to the nearest there is) is
  sent as the model's effort parameter. `none` turns a Claude's thinking off.
- Fast is not a model of its own either: a `service_tier` of `priority`
  or `fast` sends `fast=true`, anything else `fast=false` (it costs more,
  so only when asked). A model listed at a size Cursor has a fast variant
  of (served to the account) says `fast: true`, which magpie offers its
  Fast switch for (yetone/magpie#1360).
- A request goes as the picker's variant those parameters pick, in Max Mode
  when that variant is Max Mode's (a 1M size, say), as the CLI turns it on.
  A size with no variant goes in Max Mode when it is over Cursor's limit
  outside it. A model Cursor still answers "Max Mode Required" for is asked
  again in Max Mode, and so from then on.
- Hidden, Tab-only and chat-only models stay out, as in the CLI's picker.
- The usable list (`AgentService/GetUsableModels`, what `cursor-agent
  models` shows) says which variants the account has: a variant whose own
  id isn't in it is neither offered nor asked for (Sonnet 4.6 at any effort
  but medium, say), and a request for one goes as the nearest the account
  has. A model the usable list has nothing of is the picker's alone
  (GLM-5.3) and is kept whole; so is every model when Cursor can't give
  the usable list.
- A family the usable list has and the picker doesn't (an account whose
  picker lacks Claude Opus 5.5 while `cursor-agent models` lists
  `claude-opus-5-5-low` to `-max`) is listed once under its family id
  (`claude-opus-5-5`), its efforts as variants, and goes as the usable id
  those parameters pick, never as the family id Cursor doesn't know. A
  picker model whose chosen variant isn't one the account can use goes as
  its family's nearest usable id the same way. Such a family is named
  without the tier Cursor's names carry ("Claude Opus 5 1M Medium
  Thinking" is listed as Claude Opus 5 Thinking): the tier is the
  reasoning level the agent asks for (low to max, as the account has
  them), fast the request's `service_tier`.
- An id for a model with thinking that the account lists only without it
  (`claude-haiku-5-5-thinking` when the list has Claude Haiku 5.5 alone),
  or the other way round, runs as the model the account has. So does a
  picker model whose default thinks while the account lists it only
  without thinking (`claude-haiku-5-5`), or the other way round: each of
  its variant ids goes as the id the account lists.
- An `@<size>` id the list no longer has (`claude-opus-5-5@1m` when only
  300k is listed, or the model is listed unsized) runs at the model's
  nearest size, in Max Mode when the size asked for is over the model's
  window, never as the literal `@<size>` id.
- An id from before 0.2.0 still runs. A variant's own id
  (`claude-opus-5-5-high`) is that variant; a family 0.1.x listed
  (`claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-opus-5-5-fast`, `claude-haiku-5-5-thinking`,
  `cursor-grok-4.6`) is its variant nearest the default, fast for a `-fast`
  one; the picker's name for a model or a legacy slug of it is its default.
  Each is at the default context size, the request's `reasoning_effort`
  and `service_tier` counting as for a listed model. The list doesn't show
  these ids: pick the `@<size>` model for a window that is the model's.

A chat request picks its variant from the same list without waiting for it
when it needn't: a list past its 10 minutes is used while a new one is
asked for, requests at once share one ask, and after an ask fails requests
go without the list for 5 minutes instead of each waiting for it again.

## Usage

magpie shows Cursor Models, Other Models and Total for the billing period.
A plan of Cursor's merged billing (`GetPlanInfo`'s `isMerged`, the newer
plans) has no Other Models pool: its included usage is one allowance every
model draws on, as the dashboard's "Weekly usage limit" shows it. magpie
shows that as one window, Weekly (Monthly on a monthly plan), for every
model.
Accounts with a Grok Bot allowance also show its usage and reset time;
active trials are labelled separately. A spent Bot allowance doesn't stop
Cursor requests.

An account that may spend on-demand once its included usage is gone (a
team or personal spend limit, as `cursor-agent`'s usage view shows it) also
shows On-demand: its spend, and its limit when it has one. Cursor keeps
serving such an account past the included usage, so magpie doesn't count
it used up when Cursor Models or Other Models reach 100%; it does when the
on-demand spend reaches its limit. A team member with no limit of their
own spends the team's pool: On-demand shows the pool's spend and limit,
with the member's own spend beside it, and the account is used up when
the pool is.

Free credit shows too, as Cursor's own IDE reads it. The plan's bonus
("+$X free usage on us", `GetCurrentPeriodUsage`'s `bonusSpend` and
`remainingBonus`) is Free usage: what was spent from it this period, and
whether more is left; Cursor gives no amount for it. Each credit grant
(`GetUsageLimitStatusAndActiveGrants`' `activeGrants`, the IDE's "Use your
$X free credits") is a window of its own, named by its campaign: spent of
total, when it expires, and its limits. A grant limited to some models
lists them; one only Cursor's Cloud Agents (or another client) may spend
says so in its name, since magpie talks as `cursor-agent`. While a bonus
or a grant magpie can spend has some left, a spent included pool doesn't
count the account used up for the models it pays for. With "Included
usage only" on, free credit is shown only.

An Enterprise account's period has no Cursor Models, Other Models or Total
in `GetCurrentPeriodUsage`: Cursor reports its overall allowance through
the website's `usage-summary` instead. Magpie shows that as Enterprise,
for example `49.45 / 800 USD · 6.2% used`, or
`750.55 / 800 USD · 93.8% left` with Magpie's Used / Left choice, reset at
the billing cycle's end. When the summary says team on-demand is enabled
and unlimited or still has room, the Enterprise window is informational:
reaching its included allowance doesn't count the account as used up.
On-demand also shows the team's spend when known, with its limit when it
has one. A reached on-demand limit counts the account as used up.

### Included usage only (optional)

In magpie, open the Cursor provider, turn on **Included usage only** under
**Plugin options**, and save (or set `"pluginOptions": {"cursor":
{"included_only": true}}` in magpie's settings.json). It is off by default,
applies to every Cursor account, and takes effect at each account's next
usage reading.

When on, Cursor Models and Other Models (a merged plan's Weekly, an
Enterprise account's allowance) are what keep an account in routing: once one is used up, magpie moves its
models to the next account until the period resets, even when on-demand
could still pay for them. On-demand and Total are still shown but never
keep an account in routing. Use it when on-demand is a shared or paid pool
you don't want spent. When off, on-demand works as described above.

### Wire trace (optional, for bug reports)

In magpie, open the Cursor provider, turn on **Wire trace** under **Plugin
options**, and save (or set `"pluginOptions": {"cursor": {"wire_trace":
true}}` in magpie's settings.json). It is off by default and takes effect
at the next request.

When on, each Cursor request that fails (not one you cancel) saves a JSON
file in the `cursor-traces` folder of magpie's folder: `~/.config/magpie/cursor-traces`
(on Windows `C:\Users\<you>\.config\magpie\cursor-traces`), or the
portable data folder. The newest 20 are kept. A file holds the Run's
frames in order, both ways, as each frame's time (ms from the Run's
start), size, kind (text, thinking, checkpoint, heartbeat, ...), field
numbers and sizes, and the field numbers and sizes one level inside them,
plus the error and the model id. A few of Cursor's numbers are kept too: a
tool count's value, which kind of call (the field number of Cursor's tool
call) a call update is about, how many calls a checkpoint waits on, and,
for a Run that went without the native session, why. No prompt, reply or thinking text, tool
name or argument, blob or checkpoint content, token, header, account or
conversation id is written; the error's message has anything shaped like
an email, id or token taken out. Look the file over before you attach it.

Turn it off again when you're done.

Sign in to the Cursor account linked in Grok Bot. A linked SuperGrok
subscription grants Bot access without a paid Cursor plan; see
[Grok Bot plans and billing](https://cursor.com/help/grok-bot/plans).

## Not included

- Web search: Cursor's own web search is refused like its other tools.
- Switching between several accounts. OpenCode keeps one sign-in per
  provider.
- The Responses and Messages APIs: only chat completions are answered.

# @magpie-community/opencode-devin-auth

Signs in to a [Devin](https://devin.ai) subscription, the account the
`devin` CLI uses, and makes its requests, in OpenCode and in magpie.
Provider id: `devin`.

## Signing in

An account is the CLI's session token (`devin-session-token$…`). There are
two ways to get one:

- **Devin (browser)**: the CLI's own `devin auth login`, run by the
  plugin. It is a PKCE sign-in through `app.devin.ai/auth/cli/continue`
  back to a callback on `127.0.0.1`. The code is exchanged for the token
  at `server.codeium.com` (`ExchangeDevinCLIPKCECode`).
- **Devin CLI's sign-in**: takes the account the CLI is signed in to, from
  its `credentials.toml` (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/devin/`, by default
  `~/.local/share/devin/`; `%APPDATA%\devin\` on Windows). The file is only
  read, never changed.

The plugin names the account as Devin does when asked with the token
(`GetUserStatus`: its email, organization when named, and tier). When Devin can't tell, and the CLI
is installed, it asks `devin auth status`, run with a data folder of the
plugin's own, `~/.cache/opencode-devin-auth/<hash of the token>/`, so the
CLI's own sign-in is never touched. A CLI that reads another
`credentials.toml` than that folder's (on Windows it reads
`%APPDATA%\devin\` whatever it is run with) isn't asked: it would name
its own account. Otherwise the account is named "Devin".

The token is kept where OpenCode keeps sign-ins (`auth.json`; in magpie,
`plugin-auth.json`) as `{ "type": "api", "key", "metadata": { "email", "plan", "orgId", "teamId" } }`.
Devin doesn't expire it on a schedule, so there is nothing to refresh;
when it is refused, requests fail with a 401 saying to sign in again,
and the usage read marks the account signed out (`signIn: "expired"`), so
magpie passes over it and offers Sign in again on its row. A clean read
takes the mark off.

## Requests

Devin serves chat through Windsurf's API server, as the CLI does:
`POST https://server.codeium.com/exa.api_server_pb.ApiServerService/GetChatMessage`,
a Connect RPC in protobuf, with `Authorization: Basic <token>`.
`WINDSURF_API_SERVER_URL` moves the server, as it does for the CLI.

The plugin's `fetch` handles this:

- It turns OpenCode's chat completion into the CLI's request (devin-cli
  3000.11.3).
  - The system prompt goes at the head of the first user message.
  - Each tool's description goes there too, in a `<tool_descriptions>`
    block, and the tool is sent with a pointer to it. Devin answers "an
    internal error occurred" to some agents' tool descriptions when they
    are sent as the tools' own.
  - A tool call the conversation never answered is answered with "Tool use
    was interrupted and did not produce a result."
  - Images must be inline (`data:` URLs). The images a tool returned go
    with its result, as magpie's built-in sends them: a tool message's own
    `image_url` parts, and the ones magpie's gateway puts in the user
    message after the results ("[From the result of …]").
- A request past 8 KiB goes gzipped, as the CLI sends it (since 0.1.21,
  #275): Devin turns a body past 10 MiB away with 413.
- It turns the streamed reply back into a chat completion, streamed or
  not: text, reasoning, tool calls and usage.
- Failures keep their statuses: a refused token is a 401, a usage limit a
  429, a prompt too long for the model a 400.
- A reply with only metadata and usage is a 502, even when output tokens
  were counted. The plugin waits for actual content before opening a
  successful stream, so the gateway can try another channel.

## Models

Devin's models are families: `swe-2`, `claude-opus-5-5`, `gpt-6-sol`, …
Each family has variants at each effort (`swe-2-high`,
`claude-opus-5-5-xhigh`), and some have a fast or priority run
(`claude-opus-5-5-high-fast`). The plugin lists each family once, with
the efforts its variants are at, plus its fast or priority run
(`claude-opus-5-5-fast`). The variant asked for is the one at the effort
picked, or the nearest the family has; with none picked, the family's
default. Variants at no effort (`glm-5-2-1m`) are listed as they are.
Adaptive and Fusion aren't listed; they route between models inside
Devin's own agent.

The `config` hook declares Devin's list as of 2026-10-14 (89 models).
Once signed in, the `provider.models` hook replaces it with the account's
own: what Devin tells the CLI's model picker for the account's token
(`GetCliModelConfigs`, the list `devin models list` prints), with or
without the CLI and on every system. When Devin can't be asked, the list
is the CLI's `devin models list`, if the CLI names the account Devin names
the token's (on Windows it reads its own sign-in whatever folder it is
given, so it answers only for that account); else the declared list. The
list is cached for 5 minutes; after a failed read, the plugin tries again
after 1 minute.

Which models take images is what Devin tells its CLI's model picker
(`GetCliModelConfigs`, each model's `supports_images`), asked once signed
in, with or without the CLI, and cached as the list is: `swe-2`, `swe-1.7`
and most others do; GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Inkling, Nemotron, DeepSeek V4 Flash
and V4 Pro don't. Before Devin is asked, or when it can't be, the declared
list says what Devin said on 2026-10-05. A model Devin says nothing of
takes models.dev's word.

## Not included

magpie's built-in Devin account does more than this plugin:

- **Usage**: the plan's quota windows.
- **Several accounts** at once.
- **Web search**: its stand-in for Anthropic's server-side web search tool.

@magpie-community/opencode-factory-auth.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-factory-auth

Signs in to a [Factory](https://factory.ai) (Droid) subscription and sends
model requests to Factory's API the way `droid` sends them. Provider id:
`factory`.

## Sign-in

- **Sign in with Factory (device code).** This is WorkOS's device flow
  under droid's own client. The browser opens Factory's page with the code
  filled in. Confirm it there, and the plugin picks up the tokens.
- **Factory API key.** A key (`fk-…`), as droid takes one from
  `FACTORY_API_KEY`. It is sent as the bearer token with droid's headers
  and never renewed. A key carries no organization header; `whoami`, asked
  once with the key, says whose it is and where its organization is served.
- **Organization.** A token that isn't in an organization yet is put in
  the first one your account belongs to.
- **Whoami.** The plugin asks `whoami` for your active organization, its
  region (EU orgs go to `api.eu.factory.ai`) and any host of the org's
  own. Every request then carries them, as droid's do.

## Where the sign-in is kept

The sign-in is kept wherever the host keeps provider sign-ins:

- OpenCode: `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`
- magpie: `plugin-auth.json`

It holds WorkOS's access and refresh tokens, with the organization,
region and host.

**Refreshing.**
- magpie renews the access token three minutes before it lapses, through
  the plugin's `auth.refresh`, once for the account and before its
  requests and usage need it; magpie saves the new tokens. OpenCode
  doesn't call that hook: there the token is renewed two minutes before it
  lapses, before a request, and the plugin saves it.
- WorkOS rotates the refresh token, so the plugin never runs two refreshes
  at once, and never spends one refresh token twice: a request that comes
  before magpie has saved a renewal goes on with the new tokens.
- The account counts as signed out only when WorkOS refuses the refresh
  token (a 4xx other than 429). Any other failure keeps the sign-in, and
  the current token is used while it lasts.

**Refusals.** If Factory refuses the organization a request names, the
plugin asks `whoami` again and resends the request once. If the refusal
stands, the error says what to check.

## Requests from other agents

Factory serves a subscription's model requests to Droid. Every request
droid sends opens its system prompt with "You are Droid, an AI software
engineering agent built by Factory.", so another agent's request to
Factory's OpenAI-shaped API (`/api/llm/o`: GPT and Grok on Responses, the
open models on chat completions) opens with that line too, the agent's own
prompt after it. On Anthropic's Messages (`/api/llm/a`), the plugin adapts
fixed client metadata while preserving the task instructions and history;
see [Claude Code through magpie](#claude-code-through-magpie) below.

## Models

Each model is served on the one API droid uses for it:

| API | Models |
|---|---|
| Anthropic Messages (`/api/llm/a`) | Fable 5.1, Fable 5, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8 (each also in Fast Mode), Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 5.5, Haiku 4.5, MiniMax M2.7 |
| OpenAI Responses (`/api/llm/o/v1`) | GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Sol/Astra/Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.3-Codex (each also in Fast Mode), Grok 4.7, Grok 4.6 |
| Chat completions (`/api/llm/o/v1`) | GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3-Flash, GLM-5.2, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Qwen3.8 Max, MiniMax M3, Mistral Large 4, Mistral Medium 3.5, Nemotron 3 Ultra |
| Gemini generate (`/api/llm/g/v1/generate`) | Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.8/3.7/3.6/3.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Flash |

Reasoning efforts are the variants droid offers for each model. DeepSeek V4.1
Flash (1017 too), Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2 have `none`, droid's "off": they stop
thinking.
Reasoning is mandatory on GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash (Fireworks turns `none`
away), so `low` is their least.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (`deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`) is a separate model
entry, with droid 0.251.0's 1,040,000-token context, 131,072-token output,
image support, `none`/`low`/`high`/`max` efforts and 0.12x token multiplier.
Like every other model here it goes to its registry's default upstream,
`apiProviders[0]`, which is Fireworks, as droid sends it with
`x-provider-routing-source: registry_default`. Factory gates 1017 with a
feature flag, so availability still depends on the account.

A model's price is its token multiplier in droid's registry
(`cost.tokenMultiplier`), which magpie shows beside the model as its rate
(`0.8×`), so a cheap one is picked without opening droid. A promotion running
comes off it, with the multiplier before the discount struck through beside
the price (`rateWas`): Mistral Large 4's launch discount, Gemini 4 Argon's,
Gemini 3.8/3.7 Flash's and GPT-5.6 Sol's, each while droid's own dates for it
hold. A promotion that has ended is no discount at all.

Gemini's requests go to Factory's generate route with the model in the
body, droid's line opening the system instruction. Gemini 4 Argon is behind
a Factory feature flag in droid 0.241.1, so an account it isn't on for may
be refused it.

A Fast Mode model (`claude-opus-5-5-fast`, `gpt-5.5-fast`, …) is its base
model served faster, for more of the plan's credits. It goes out as droid
sends it: its own id, with `speed: "fast"` and the `fast-mode-2026-02-01`
beta on Anthropic's API, at `service_tier: "priority"` on OpenAI's. A request
that asks the base model for fast (Claude Code's `speed: "fast"`, a
Responses request's `service_tier: "priority"`) is sent to its Fast Mode
model, as droid's own fast toggle does: asked of the base model, Factory
answered at standard speed (#119). Opus 4.6/4.7 Fast, GPT-5.4 Mini Fast, GPT-5.6 Sol Fast (unreleased)
and GLM-5.2 Fast (behind a feature flag) are not included.

auto is not included: droid picks it on the client side.

## Requests too large

Factory refuses a request body over its size limit with 413 "Request
Entity Too Large". The limit is on bytes, not on the model's context, and
images reach it first. On a 413 the plugin sends the request once more with
every image and file but the newest replaced by a line saying it was left
out, each tool result kept beside its call, as droid does. If that is still
too large, or there was nothing to leave out, the error says it is
Factory's byte limit: compact the conversation or start a new one.

## Use

```sh
magpie plugin add @magpie-community/opencode-factory-auth
magpie plugin login factory
```

## Standard usage only (optional)

In magpie, open the Factory provider, turn on **Standard usage only** under
**Plugin options**, and save (or set `"pluginOptions": {"factory":
{"standard_only": true}}` in magpie's settings.json). It is off by default,
applies to every Factory account, and takes effect at each account's next
usage reading.

When on, the plugin reports the Standard 5 hours, 7 days and 30 days
windows as counting every model, Droid Core's open models too, whether or
not the account has Extra usage. Droid Core's windows and Extra usage are
still shown but never keep an account in routing.

magpie leaves an account out before sending only when it is held at a
usage cap, so pair the option with a cap on each account, for example
`magpie provider account-cap factory <account> 99`. An account is then
skipped once any Standard window reaches the cap, the request goes to the
next account with the same model, and when every account is held magpie
answers 429 without sending. Without a cap, an account whose Standard
usage is gone is still tried, and Factory may serve a Droid Core model
from Core or Extra usage. Readings lag, so the last requests before a
window fills still go out; to never spend Extra usage, turn it off in
Factory.

## Claude Code through magpie

Factory's Anthropic route requires Droid's fixed client preamble and
refuses some of Claude Code's fixed environment, model and built-in skill
metadata. The plugin adapts that metadata while preserving the coding
instructions, environment values, tool definitions, images and reasoning
options. Ordinary Droid requests remain unchanged, and OpenAI routes keep
their existing request adapter. Quoted fixed metadata in tool results is
handled as described below.
The fixed Claude identity is recognized as a complete first line too when
magpie joins it with the following system instructions into one text block.

For the built-in `update-config` skill, the adapter changes only the known
self-reference "not Claude" to "not the assistant" inside that skill's entry
in a generated skill list. Claude Code renders the entry two ways: as a
system message (`- update-config: …`) and, in the `claude-code-guide` agent's
own system prompt under `# User's Current Configuration`, with the slash that
invokes it (`- /update-config: …`). Both spellings are adapted, and only the
sentence Factory refuses changes, so the entry's name and the rest of the list
stay. Its configuration instructions, other skill descriptions, tools and
caller text are preserved.

Claude 5 can send runtime metadata in string-content `system` messages
instead of user-message reminders. The plugin adapts the known environment,
model and configuration-skill metadata in that shape too, preserving the
message role, environment values and session instructions.
Startup hooks (`SessionStart` or `SubagentStart`, including additional
context) and deferred-tool announcements may precede that environment
block. The adapter preserves the prefix verbatim and adapts the generated
runtime context after it, including when folded into user text.
After `/model` switches, Claude Code can send model-only system updates
without the initial environment paragraph. Updates beginning with the known
model paragraph and containing complete generated token metadata are
adapted too, including accumulated switches when resuming a conversation.
Token budgets, permission instructions and conversation history are preserved.
The same model-update adaptation covers updates that start with the complete
generated `# Environment update` block after a working-directory change.

Claude Code's generated compaction summaries also have a fixed opening
that Factory refuses. The adapter recognizes the two generated opening
sentences and rephrases only the first in user strings and text blocks,
including summaries without a `Summary:` label. The generated artifact
provenance marker and note stay verbatim. If the summary itself quotes any
of the refused client phrases handled in tool output, the context after the
two opening sentences is encoded as a JSON string with explicit decoding
instructions. Decoding restores the exact summary, transcript path and
continuation instructions; context without those phrases stays verbatim.
Complete generated reminders for restored Read calls and omitted files are
adapted too. Read arguments and file paths are preserved; quoted or incomplete
reminders are left alone.
Claude Code (2.1.291 and later) also restores skills invoked before compaction
as one generated reminder. Factory refuses that fixed opening, and the restored
skill text can quote the same client phrases as tool output. A complete
reminder has its opening sentence rephrased. When its skill text quotes a
refused phrase, that text is encoded as a JSON string with explicit skill-text
decoding instructions; decoding restores the skill text exactly. Skill text
without those phrases stays verbatim inside the rephrased reminder. Pasted
fragments and incomplete reminders are left untouched.
Claude Code can also combine reminders into a token-prefixed `system` turn
without the reminder wrappers. The adapter handles the known metadata
paragraphs in that form, including skill-list updates and complete
invoked-skills reminders. A complete reminder is the fixed opening sentence
followed by the complete `IMPORTANT:` paragraph; skill text then runs until
the next known attachment (a token marker, hook, restored Read, omitted-file
note, Read result, environment, model line, skill-list header, changed-file
note, agent-type list or MCP server instructions) or the end of the turn.
Numbered file contents, token markers and SessionStart hook output stay.
The same adaptation applies when a translating gateway folds that complete
token-prefixed block into a user message.
Standalone skill updates can instead start with the generated skill-list
header and end with a token marker, for example when leaving auto mode.
That complete form receives the same adaptation while retaining the skill
descriptions and mode-change instructions.
The skill list can also come alone as a `system` message, with only its
entries: no header, no reminder wrapper and no token marker, as text blocks
or a string. A `system` message that opens with an entry gets the same
change to the known `update-config` line; everything else in it stays.
When runtime notifications precede the skill update, the adapter recognizes
the complete skill-header and bullet-list paragraphs inside a token-terminated
bundle. It preserves MCP connection errors, other notifications, mode updates
and custom skill descriptions while adapting the known built-in description.
After `/compact`, Claude Code also sends the files it restores and the
runtime context as one turn that opens with an unwrapped restored-file note,
Read call or complete invoked-skills reminder, with no token marker first.
A complete skills reminder is recognized even when no files were restored
and no environment or token paragraph follows it. A restored-file opening
requires the generated environment paragraph, a token marker or a complete
skills reminder before any hook output. Each fixed paragraph (file notes,
Read calls and results, skills, environment, model line) is adapted as in a
token-prefixed bundle; everything else stays byte-for-byte. Quoted,
incomplete and hook-owned forms are left alone.

Factory can also refuse fixed client phrases quoted in tool results, such as
the identity/environment definitions printed when inspecting this plugin's
source, the compaction opening embedded in a historical session JSONL
record, or pi's opening sentence in a model snapshot of its own system
prompt. Those text results are represented as JSON strings with explicit
decoding instructions and Unicode escapes for the fixed phrases. Decoding
the string recovers the exact original output, including quotes, backslashes
and Unicode; the plugin does not delete the output or replace its identities
with different ones. Tool ids, cache/error markers and non-text blocks stay
unchanged. Ordinary tool results are forwarded as before.
The same lossless encoding applies to restored or `@`-attached Read file text
after the exact `Result of calling the Read tool:` header, including complete
reminder wrappers and announced runtime bundles. The generated header and
wrapper stay intact. File text without a known refused phrase is unchanged.
Claude Code's complete changed-on-disk notifications receive the same handling:
only the numbered file snippet is encoded, retaining its TAB or colon line
separators, hunk separators and truncation notice. The path and instructions
about respecting the current file stay verbatim. This covers wrapped user
attachments and generated system bundles, including notifications before a
token marker. Changed-file text supplied by hooks, quoted or incomplete
notifications, and notices that omit the snippet are left alone. Model and
environment metadata after non-startup hooks retain their existing adaptation.

Claude Code's instructions reminder names `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` "(user's
private global instructions for all projects)", which Factory refuses; in
the generated reminder it becomes "(global instructions)". Claude Code
renders that reminder two ways: the first copy opens with "Codebase and user
instructions are shown below", and a copy re-read after the files changed
(after compaction, a settings sync and the like) opens with "Instruction
files were re-read …; these differ from their earlier copies" or "These
instruction files changed". Both are adapted, in text blocks, string user
turns and chat completions' joined user text; text after the reminder and
a user's own mention of the phrase stay as written. A tool result that
quotes the phrase (reading Claude Code's renderer, say) gets the lossless
JSON encoding above.

When Factory still answers 403, the error magpie and the agent see keeps
Factory's request id (from `x-request-id`, `request-id` or `cf-ray`, or the
body) and its error code and type, and the Anthropic-route body carries
`request_id`, so the refusal can be named to Factory.

Use magpie's Claude Code integration to select the Factory provider.
magpie manages the provider-specific client settings, including capability
and permission configuration. Fields such as `safeguards` and
`context_management` are forwarded for Factory to validate; the request
adapter preserves them along with the other request options. One exception:
Factory's streaming route refuses `context_management` ("Extra inputs are
not permitted") while its non-streaming route takes it, so a streamed
request is sent without it. The server then clears nothing from the
context; Claude Code's own compaction still runs.

The same metadata adaptation applies to `/messages` and
`/messages/count_tokens`, so token counting sees the prompt used for
inference. Serving the counting endpoint still depends on the host and
upstream. Model and feature availability depend on the Factory account,
organization region and upstream API. Connectivity has been verified with
Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5. Two-turn Read tool calls with Claude
Code's default tool set have been verified with Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 5.5,
including Sonnet 5.5 selected through a routing group.

## Tool schema compatibility

Factory's Anthropic route rejects tool schemas with root-level `anyOf`,
`oneOf` or `allOf`. The plugin nests those schemas under an internal
`arguments` property instead of removing their branch constraints. It
wraps examples and previous tool inputs too, then unwraps tool replies
before returning them to OpenCode or magpie. Ordinary object schemas and
OpenAI routes keep their existing behavior.

Local schema pointers are rebased to the nested schema; `$id` resources
and anchors retain their resolution scope, and literal data is unchanged.
Recursive schema resources
without `$id` fail explicitly because nesting would change their scope.
Affected streaming tool arguments are buffered until their content block
is complete. Other events, tool ids, usage and upstream errors pass through;
an incomplete or invalid argument envelope fails instead of being executed.

@magpie-community/opencode-gcp-ai-auth.readme:
# GCP AI — Google Cloud credits and Vertex models (Magpie / OpenCode plugin)

- **Models**: the Vertex chat models your project can call, newest first.
- **Inference**: requests speak Gemini's own protocol (`@ai-sdk/google`) to the project's Vertex endpoint, signed with your local gcloud / ADC credentials and billed to your own project.
- **Credits**: the quota panel can show your Google Cloud promotional credit balance and its expiry date.

You sign in once with your own Google account. No service accounts, no JSON keys, no extra packages: the plugin uses the Chrome you already have.

## Requirements

- Google Chrome or Chromium (set `VERTEX_CHROME_PATH` if it is somewhere unusual)
- Google Cloud CLI (`gcloud`), already working — on Windows the `gcloud.cmd` the installer puts on `PATH` is used
- A Google Cloud project with Vertex AI enabled
- To read credits: permission to view the project's billing account (usually `billing.viewer`)

Linux has been tried with real accounts. Support for macOS and Windows is
implemented, but has not been tried with a real account on either platform.
On Windows the plugin's own files live under `%APPDATA%` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%`
instead of `~/.config` and `~/.cache`, and gcloud is
started through `cmd.exe`, which is the only way Windows runs a `.cmd`.

## What this was run on

Sign-in, model listing and a real inference request were run on **Linux** against
**two real Google accounts**, with gcloud's own ADC and with an ADC the plugin wrote.

The Windows path — `cmd.exe` for `gcloud.cmd`, `%APPDATA%`/`%LOCALAPPDATA%` for the
plugin's own files — is implemented and covered by the unit tests' path handling, but
**has not been run on a Windows machine with a real account**. If it misbehaves there,
that is why; macOS has likewise not been tried with a real account.

## Install and sign in

```bash
magpie plugin add @magpie-community/gcp-ai
```

Then click sign in on the **GCP AI** row, or run:

```bash
magpie plugin login gcp-ai
```

One Chrome window opens. Approve the consent page there and the plugin closes the window itself — never close it yourself.

- The first account goes straight to Google's consent page. Adding a second one starts on Google's account picker instead, in the same window.
- Add another account by clicking sign in again with a different Google account.
- The project is picked for you: the first of the account's projects with the Vertex AI API enabled.
- If the account already has an ADC here, nothing is added and your existing sign-in is left alone.

## Credits

Google has no API for promotional credits, so the balance is read from the Cloud Console page. The row opens a browser when it needs a balance, and only then. Balances are cached for five minutes.

## What it keeps where

- **Credentials**: never held by the plugin. gcloud writes them and prints tokens on demand.
- **ADC directories**: `<config>/gcp-ai/adc-<account>`, one per Google account. The plugin never writes gcloud's own directory. Two addresses that differ only in punctuation would share a directory name, so the second one gets a short hash of its address appended.
- **Chrome profile**: `<config>/gcp-auto-profile`.
- **Cache**: `<cache>/magpie/gcp-ai`.

`<config>` is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, else `%APPDATA%` on Windows, else `~/.config`. `<cache>` is
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME`, else `%LOCALAPPDATA%` on Windows, else `~/.cache`.

## FAQ

**No credits shown?** The Chrome sign-in has probably expired. Sign in again.

**"This browser or app may not be secure"?** Start the sign-in again from the row and use the window that opens. Nothing in it is automated.

**"That account was already signed in"?** Signing in adds an account; it does not refresh one. Use a different Google account.

**Wrong account on the consent page?** Sign in again and pick the right one. Nothing that was already here is removed.

**Credits don't match the billing page?** Promotional credits belong to the billing account and can be shared across projects, and the Console has billing latency.

## Configuration

| Environment variable | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `GOOGLE_VERTEX_LOCATION` | `global` |
| `VERTEX_BILLING_ACCOUNT` | Looked up from the project |
| `VERTEX_CHROME_PROFILE` | `~/.config/gcp-auto-profile` |
| `VERTEX_CHROME_PATH` | Detected |
| `VERTEX_GCLOUD_ACCOUNT` | The signed-in account |
| `VERTEX_GCLOUD_AUTH_MODE` | `auto`; also `adc` or `gcloud` |
| `VERTEX_CHROME_IDLE` | `30` seconds a kept browser waits before closing; `0` closes it right away |
| `VERTEX_CHROME_GAP` | `0` seconds between one process closing Chrome and the next opening the profile |
| `VERTEX_CREDITS_CACHE_TTL` | `300` seconds |
| `VERTEX_CREDITS_FAILURE_TTL` | `1200` seconds |
| `VERTEX_CREDITS_TRANSIENT_TTL` | `60` seconds, for network failures |
| `VERTEX_MODELS_CACHE_TTL` | `21600` seconds (6 hours) |

A machine-wide `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG` is never read. It would point every account at one ADC, and a sign-in there would overwrite credentials the plugin didn't write; the plugin only uses its own `<config>/gcp-ai/adc-<account>` directories.

## Privacy

The plugin asks Google for your model list with your credentials, sends inference requests to the Vertex endpoint, and opens Cloud Console in a Chrome it started to read your credits. No third-party server, no credential upload, no debugging port.

@magpie-community/opencode-grok-auth.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-grok-auth

Grok with a SuperGrok or X Premium+ subscription, through the sign-in of
xAI's [Grok Build CLI](https://x.ai/cli). Provider id: `grok`.

It needs Grok Build installed:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh | bash          # macOS, Linux
irm https://x.ai/cli/install.ps1 | iex                 # Windows
```

It is found in the installer's folder (`GROK_BIN_DIR`, `GROK_HOME/bin`,
`~/.grok/bin`), or on `PATH` when it lives under a `.grok` folder, so that
another program named `grok` isn't taken for it. Where the installer can't
run, such as a container without curl, put the binary in a folder of your
own and set `GROK_BIN_DIR` to it. magpie installs Grok Build itself, as
the installer does, before a sign-in that needs it.

## Sign in

- **Sign in with Grok Build (device code)** runs `grok login --device-auth`
  and opens the page it prints. Approve the sign-in there, and the CLI
  finishes it.
  - If the CLI isn't signed in yet, the sign-in goes to the CLI's own home
    (`GROK_HOME`, else `~/.grok`), as if you had run `grok login`.
  - If it is signed in, the sign-in goes to a home of this plugin's,
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode-grok-auth/<random>` (else under
    `~/.config`). Grok Build's own sign-in stays as it is.
  - The account is told apart by its email, else its xAI user id (an
    account signed in through X can have no email). `GROK_AUTH_PATH` is
    left out of the CLI's run, so the sign-in lands in that home.
  - When the CLI finishes but leaves no sign-in there, the failure says
    which file it read and what it found.
- **Use Grok Build's current sign-in** takes the account the CLI is
  signed in to, with nothing to approve.
- **Import CPA Grok account JSON** copies one enabled xAI OAuth account from
  a CLIProxyAPI (CPA) account JSON file (CPA keeps it as
  `~/.cli-proxy-api/xai-<email>.json`) into a private home for this plugin.
  CPA and Grok Build rotate the same refresh token, so stop using that
  account in CPA before importing it. The file is read, never rewritten.

## Where the sign-in is kept

The CLI keeps the sign-in in its home, as `auth.json`. OpenCode (or
magpie) keeps where that home is, the token and its expiry. Importing a CPA
account writes only its translated xAI OAuth fields to a private home owned
by this plugin; the selected CPA file is left unchanged.

The plugin reads `auth.json`; Grok Build refreshes the token, which changes
each time. The plugin runs `grok models` in that home, so the CLI renews
it, then reads it again:

- magpie renews the token 5 minutes before it ends, through the plugin's
  `auth.refresh`, once for the account and before its requests, models
  and usage need it. magpie saves what the CLI gave.
- OpenCode doesn't call that hook: there the token is renewed when it is
  5 minutes from expiring, before a request.
- The CLI runs once for a home at a time: a request or renewal that
  comes while it runs waits for it and reads what it gave. A token the
  CLI already renewed is taken as it is.
- Grok can turn a token away before its `expires_at`. A request, model
  list or usage read that gets 401 has the CLI renew the token and asks
  once more with the new one.
- When the CLI's run leaves the token as it was, the 401 or error says
  Grok Build couldn't renew the sign-in, with what the CLI said. For Grok
  Build's own home ("Use Grok Build's current sign-in") opening Grok Build
  and sending it a message renews it. For a home of the plugin's (a second
  account, an imported one), opening Grok Build doesn't touch it: add the
  account in magpie again.
- When the CLI no longer holds a sign-in in that home (`grok logout`),
  the account has to be signed in again. When it couldn't renew a token
  that has ended, magpie tries again later.
- An `auth.json` that is empty or not JSON is most likely one the CLI is
  writing: it is read again for about half a second, then the last sign-in
  read whole there stands, as the CLI itself keeps its previous one. It is
  never taken as signed out. The plugin takes no `auth.json.lock`.

## Requests

Requests go to `https://cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1`, OpenAI's Responses
API (`@ai-sdk/openai`), signed as the CLI signs them:

- `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- `x-xai-token-auth: xai-grok-cli`
- `x-grok-client-identifier: grok-shell`
- `x-grok-client-mode: headless`
- `x-grok-client-version` and `User-Agent: grok-shell/<version> (<os>; <arch>)`.
  The version is 1.0.41, or the installed CLI's if it is newer.
- `x-grok-model-override`: the request's model. A window suffix
  (`grok-4.7@500k`) is the plain model (`grok-4.7`) here and in the body.
- `x-grok-context-window`: the token count a suffixed model names
  (`500000` for `@500k`). The plain id sends no such header and stays on
  the default window.
- `x-grok-conv-id`: the request's `prompt_cache_key`.
- `x-grok-doom-loop-check: 1024` and `x-grok-exact-repetition-check: 64`
  on a Responses request, as Grok Build sends them: the proxy then stops a
  reply that repeats itself after ~1K tokens instead of letting it run on.

The backend turns away some of what a request may carry, so the plugin
leaves these out:

- tools of types it doesn't take (a freeform `apply_patch`, namespaces)
- `external_web_access` on web search
- a `tool_choice` naming a dropped type
- a `tool_choice` with no tools beside it (magpie sends `"none"` so when a
  client turned tools off)
- a reasoning item's `"content": null`

Plain Codex collaboration items (`agent_message`) reach Grok as user
messages, with their sender, recipient and content preserved. Sealed or
unrecognized content stays unchanged; the plugin does not decrypt tasks.

### Native X search (optional)

In magpie, open the Grok provider, turn on **Native X search** under
**Plugin options**, and save. It is off by default; changes apply to the
next request without restarting or signing in again.

When enabled, the plugin offers Grok its native `x_search` tool. Grok
decides whether to search; enabling it does not force a search on every
request. Existing function tools and X search filters are preserved, and
an existing `x_search` is not duplicated. Explicit choices such as `none`,
`required`, a named tool, or `allowed_tools` never gain another tool.

The option applies to Responses requests, including Chat Completions,
Anthropic Messages and Gemini requests that magpie converts to Responses,
in streaming and non-streaming mode. Use magpie with the fix for
[yetone/magpie#3110](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/issues/3110) so that
those clients' tool-disable choices reach the plugin.

For compatibility with older gateways, a request that reaches the plugin
with neither tools nor a `tool_choice` is left unchanged. This can happen
when magpie translates a client's automatic choice on an empty tool list.
To use X search through a translated API, send at least one function tool;
the plugin adds X search alongside it. An explicit tool-disable choice
always takes precedence.

This uses the existing `grok` provider's login, models and quota reporting;
no extra plugin is needed. It applies to that provider's models when the
upstream supports X search, not to Grok models served through Cursor or
another provider. Report problems in
[this repository](https://github.com/magpie-community/plugins/issues).

## Models

Grok 4.7 until signed in. Signed in, the models are the ones the account
lists at `/v1/models` (Responses models only), each with its reasoning
efforts as variants.

`context_window` is the default window and keeps the plain id, so a saved
`grok-4.7` stays a 256k model. Each other size in `context_windows` is
offered beside it, named `Grok 4.7 @ 500k` with id `grok-4.7@500k` and
that many tokens as its window. A request for it sends
`x-grok-context-window: 500000`. The proxy serves up to its largest
window either way and refuses past it; the header names the window the
caller asked to compact against. Pick `grok-4.7@500k` where a client
compacts at the advertised window, such as Claude Code.

## Usage

magpie's card shows the credits of the current period
(`/v1/billing?format=credits`): weekly for SuperGrok, with on-demand
spending beside it when it has a cap.

Grok's billing says nothing of a plan's rate limit, so a free account can
read 0% used while its requests come back 429. After a 429 the card shows
a spent "Rate limit" window until the reset it named (`Retry-After`, or a
`*ratelimit*reset*` header). When it named none, the window stays until a
request goes through, or for 5 minutes.

Grok Bot's separate allowance is shown by the [Cursor plugin](../cursor/README.md#usage).
Sign in there with the Cursor account linked in Grok Bot, including for
access through SuperGrok.
