@magpie-community/opencode-workbuddy-aut.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-workbuddy-auth

Signs in to the plans of WorkBuddy, Tencent's desktop agent from CodeBuddy.
It has one provider for each of WorkBuddy's two builds:

| Provider id | Build | API |
|---|---|---|
| `workbuddy` | WorkBuddy, the China build (CodeBuddy plan) | `https://copilot.tencent.com/v2` |
| `workbuddy-ai` | WorkBuddy AI, the international build | `https://www.workbuddy.ai/v2` |

The package exports `WorkBuddyAuthPlugin` (`workbuddy`) and
`WorkBuddyAIAuthPlugin` (`workbuddy-ai`).

## Signing in

- **Account (browser).** Opens Tencent's sign-in page for the build, the
  one WorkBuddy's desktop app opens. The plugin then asks WorkBuddy for the
  token every second until you're signed in, for 5 minutes at most. Nothing
  needs to be pasted.
- **Desktop's sign-in.** Uses the account WorkBuddy desktop is signed in
  to. Nothing is copied: the app's file is read on each request, and never
  changed:
  - macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/CodeBuddyExtension/Data/Public/auth/workbuddy-desktop[-ai].info`
  - Windows: `~/AppData/Local/CodeBuddyExtension/…`
  - Linux: `~/.local/share/CodeBuddyExtension/…`

  WorkBuddy 5.6 and later keep the sign-in encrypted, which only the app
  opens, so this way fails there and says so: use the browser sign-in.
- **API key** (since 0.1.37). A key made on the build's own keys page
  (`https://www.workbuddy.cn/profile/keys` for `workbuddy`,
  `https://www.workbuddy.ai/profile/keys` for `workbuddy-ai`), sent as
  WorkBuddy's own CLI sends one: `X-API-Key` and `Authorization: Bearer`,
  both the key, and `X-User-Id: anonymous_<the key's last 8 characters>`,
  to the same API as the other sign-ins. A key isn't renewed; a refused one
  says to check it. A key's credits are unknown (WorkBuddy's own client reads
  none with a key), and its models are `/v3/config`'s only for `ck_`/`pt_`
  keys, as the CLI asks; any other key keeps the list below.

A browser sign-in is kept as an OpenCode `oauth` auth: the access and
refresh tokens, their expiry, the user id and the domain; desktop's as a
marker, `{"type": "oauth", "source": "desktop", "accountId", "uid"}`. OpenCode keeps it in
`auth.json`; magpie keeps it in `plugin-auth.json`. The access token is
refreshed a minute before it ends, and the new one is saved. If the refresh
fails, the old token is used while it lasts.

In magpie (0.1.684 or later) the plugin also gives `auth.refresh` with
`refreshLead` of 5 minutes: magpie renews a browser sign-in (an hour's
token) 5 minutes before it ends, once for the account, before its
requests, models and usage ask, and saves what it gives. It goes through
the same one-refresh-at-a-time as a request's refresh, so a refresh token
is never spent twice. A failed renewal, a refresh token past its end
included, doesn't mark the account, as the built-in never did; magpie
tries again later, and the old token is used meanwhile.
OpenCode doesn't call `auth.refresh`; the check before each request stays.

An enterprise (team) account is asked for as the enterprise. A browser
sign-in keeps the enterprise id WorkBuddy names for the account (from
`/login/account`, else its account list), and desktop's is read from the
app's file. Every request then carries `X-Enterprise-Id` and `X-Tenant-Id`,
as WorkBuddy's own client sends them; without them WorkBuddy answers as the
personal account, with the personal plan's models. A browser sign-in made
before 0.1.13 has no enterprise id kept: sign in again.

Which account a browser sign-in gives is chosen on WorkBuddy's own sign-in
page. After a phone sign-in it lists the person's accounts (personal, a
team, 「WorkBuddy 教育公益版」…) and binds the one picked to the sign-in, so
to add an education or team account, pick it there. Its account is named
with the enterprise too (`nickname · enterprise name`, or the end of the
enterprise id when WorkBuddy names none): one person's personal and
enterprise accounts share the uid and the nickname, and magpie keeps one
account per name and uid, so before 0.2.1 signing in to the enterprise
account replaced the personal one. An enterprise account signed in before
0.2.1 keeps its old name until its Sign in again, which renames it in
place; its free-model window, read from usage rows kept under the old
name, starts again from the new one.

Desktop's sign-in is refreshed only when the app hasn't refreshed it
itself, and the new token is kept in memory, never written back, as magpie's
built-in WorkBuddy does.

A chat or usage read WorkBuddy answers 401 (since 0.1.31) is renewed once,
whatever the token's time, and sent once more. A token another process
saved since is taken first instead of spending the refresh token again. A
desktop sign-in is never renewed for it: the app's file is read again, and
its token is used if the app signed in again. A 401 again, or no new
token, ends in a 401 that says to sign in again (Providers → WorkBuddy →
this account's Sign in again in magpie; WorkBuddy desktop for a desktop
sign-in). The plugin marks the account expired in magpie
(`X-Magpie-Sign-In: expired`, usage's `signIn`) only on WorkBuddy's word
that the sign-in is gone: the refresh token refused (401, `invalid_grant`),
or the access token refused (`WWW-Authenticate: … error="invalid_token"`)
with no refresh token left to renew it with or just after renewing. A
failed renewal for another reason, or a bare 401 without `invalid_token`,
leaves the account as it is; a desktop sign-in is never marked. A 401
after a renewal takes a mark off (`renewed`).

## Requests

Chats are chat completions (`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`) at `<API>/chat/completions`.
They are streamed only; WorkBuddy refuses a chat that isn't.

**On WorkBuddy (China), the Claude models are served on Anthropic's Messages
API** instead: `@ai-sdk/anthropic` at `<endpoint>/v1/messages` (streamed only
as well). `claude-opus-5.5`, `claude-sonnet-5.5`, `claude-opus-5` and
`claude-opus-4.8-1m` answered there when each model of `/v3/config`'s `cli`
agent was asked on 2026-10-24; `glm-5.3` and `deepseek-v4.1-flash` answered
500, `gpt-5.5` and `kimi-k3-1` 400, so every other model stays on chat.
WorkBuddy AI has no such route (`/v1/messages` is `404 Route Not Found` there
for every model), so all its models stay on chat, a Claude one too.

A Messages request goes as the agent sent it: no default system message, no
`max_completion_tokens`/`developer` rewrites, no tool reshaping, and nothing
moved for a refused system prompt — Claude Code's own prompt is taken as it
is, billing line and all, where a chat answers 11128 to it. One thing is
left out: a `thinking` block with no `signature`. A conversation that began
on chat (or on another provider) carries such blocks, and once a signed one
from this route sits beside them WorkBuddy refuses the whole request, 11159
"Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block … bound to a different
conversation", on every try. Signed blocks go back as they came. It carries
WorkBuddy's headers as a chat does, the same conversation and turn ids
included: a tool result in a `user` message of `tool_result` blocks answers
the step before it, as a `role: "tool"` message does in a chat.

The point of the route is effort. A chat carries `reasoning_effort` alone,
and WorkBuddy's chat endpoint answers at about the same length whatever it
says: asked the same question four times each (2026-10-24,
`claude-opus-5.5`), the median answer was 3884 output tokens at `low`, 5144
at `max` and 5715 at a value that isn't a level at all. Messages carries
`output_config.effort`, and `max` is honored there: a median of 30850
against 5748 at `low`, same model and question, four runs each. A Claude
model on Messages therefore lists `max` in its levels even where
`/v3/config` stops at `xhigh`.

`/v1/messages/count_tokens` **is not served** (404). magpie treats a 404 on
count_tokens as "no counter" (`unsupportedCount`) and answers with its own
estimate.

Each chat carries WorkBuddy's headers:
- `Authorization`, `X-User-Id`, `X-Domain`, `X-Product: SaaS`, `X-IDE-Type: WorkBuddy`;
- the desktop CLI's `User-Agent`, `WorkBuddy/<app> <appName>/<app> CLI/<cli>`:
  `WorkBuddy/5.9.3 WorkBuddy/5.9.3 CLI/2.165.0` on the China build and
  `WorkBuddy/5.9.3 workbuddy-ai/5.9.3 CLI/2.165.0` on WorkBuddy AI, each
  build's current app on 2026-10-29; `X-IDE-Version` is the app's version.
  A User-Agent not starting `WorkBuddy/<version>` is answered error 10085;
- the client's, which WorkBuddy's usage list shows as the client that asked
  (使用端): `X-Agent-Purpose: conversation`, `X-IDE-Name: WorkBuddy`,
  `X-IDE-Version`, `X-Agent-Intent: craft`, `X-Requested-With`. Both builds
  send them, as WorkBuddy's own client does; a chat without them is counted
  under no client at all;
- the conversation's ids: `X-Conversation-ID`, `X-Conversation-Request-ID`,
  `X-Conversation-Message-ID`, `X-Request-ID`. WorkBuddy's backend counts a
  user send as one request by `X-Conversation-Request-ID`, so every step of
  one send — a tool result sent back, a retry — carries the same one, and
  the user's next message carries another. Both ids are one account's own,
  as WorkBuddy's client is signed in as one: a conversation sent as another
  account (another of a group, or a sign-in saved since) carries that
  account's ids, never the same ones under two `X-User-Id`s. The
  conversation's is the session magpie (or OpenCode) names the request by,
  else the chat's first user message; nothing is made up when neither names
  one, a made-up conversation of the request's own being what splits one
  conversation into many in the usage detail;
- what the CLI adds to a model request alone: `X-Agent-Type: main` on both
  builds, `X-Agent-Runtime: local-agent` (new in 5.9),
  `Accept: application/json`, and the `X-Stainless-*` headers of the OpenAI
  SDK it sends through (openai 6.25.0 on Electron 37's Node v22.21.1, a
  1200s timeout, no retries).

Not sent: `X-Device-Token`, which the desktop app gets from Tencent's
native device SDK before each prompt, and a `traceparent`, which the CLI
adds only while its server-side tracing is on.

A chat that doesn't open with a system message is given WorkBuddy's
default one, as the app does.

WorkBuddy refuses some agents' identity lines as an "unapproved channel"
(11128), so those lines are reworded before a chat goes out. Since 0.1.27
(#279) that includes DeepSeek Harness's opening line. Since 0.2.3 a refusal
of words not reworded yet is answered first by saying the same line with one
more comma — a vendor matches such a line whole and exactly, so the comma
passes it while the line still names the harness (measured 2026-10-30; a word
added after the product name did not pass, the comma did). The comma is set in
the system and assistant messages only — the two WorkBuddy reads — so the
user's own words and tools' results go out as they were sent. A system prompt
whose comma passed is remembered while the plugin is loaded, as a moved one
is, and its next chats go with the comma already in before the first send:
otherwise every turn, and every step of a tool loop, would pay the refusal
once. Only a chat refused still is sent once more, since 0.1.29, with the
system prompt moved into the first user message (inside `<instructions>` tags)
and WorkBuddy's default system prompt in its place: WorkBuddy checks only the
system and assistant messages, and the line it matched is then in neither. A system message later
in the chat becomes a user message where it stands. The plugin remembers each
refused system prompt while it is loaded, so that agent's next chats go moved
at once. The move can't reach an assistant message, so words the model quotes
back into one keep that chat refused until they are in the list reworded in
every message (since 0.1.30, the "Web GUI whose URL the runtime context names"
line, #291); otherwise only a new chat clears it. A refusal that stands after
the move ends in a hint that names no one client (since 0.1.28): WorkBuddy
refused words in this client's prompt; use it from Hermes, OpenCode or Pi, or
add another provider to the group. Since 0.2.3 that hint is preceded by the
address of [REFUSED.md](REFUSED.md), which says what the check reads, how a
line is reworded to pass it, and how to turn such a line off in an agent that
has a switch for it — so the error carries its own fix, for the person who
reads it or the agent they paste it to. Neither refusal rests the account.

The loader also translates OpenAI-compatible request spellings WorkBuddy
doesn't take: `max_completion_tokens` becomes `max_tokens`, `developer`
messages become `system`, an object `tool_choice` becomes WorkBuddy's
string form, and an earlier assistant turn's `reasoning_content` (or
`reasoning_details` text) goes as `reasoning`, the field WorkBuddy's own
client sends. WorkBuddy drops `reasoning_content`, so a client such as Grok
Build that sends it lost its earlier thinking; nothing is folded into the
message's content.

A chat's tools are given shapes WorkBuddy's models take. Without them
WorkBuddy AI answers 400 "Invalid request parameters" (11133), DeepSeek's
models to each shape below and Kimi's, GPT's, Gemini's and GLM's to some:
- a tool's parameters with no `type`, empty, or a union (`anyOf`, `oneOf`,
  `allOf`) at the root are an object, the union's fields merged;
- a `pattern`'s `\0` is `\u0000`, which matches the same;
- a tuple's `items` (a list) is one schema any of them fits;
- an `enum` with no `type` takes its values' type (or that and `"null"`),
  and an `enum` of several types is an `anyOf` of one typed `enum` for
  each, at any depth; an empty `enum` is left out (Kimi and DeepSeek, an
  MCP server's tools, #122);
- `true` and `false` where a schema goes are `{}` and `{"not": {}}`
  (`additionalProperties` is left); a `required` that isn't a list, and a
  `type` JSON Schema doesn't name, are left out, and `"String"` is
  `"string"`;
- a tool's name with a character other than letters, digits, `_` and `-`
  (`.`, `:`, `/`, a space, CJK) is sent with `_` there, and the model's
  calls come back under the tool's own name.

WorkBuddy AI's `gemini-3.8-flash` answers 400 "the conversation must end
with a user message" (11153) to a chat whose tool results are followed by
the user's message, as magpie sends Claude Code's reminders, words typed
mid-task and a tool's images. Such a chat goes again with an empty
assistant message between the results and the user's message, which it
serves; a model that refused it once gets it that way from then on, until
the plugin restarts. A chat ending with the assistant's message (a prefill)
is refused as before.

WorkBuddy's safety filter can refuse a reply it has begun:
`deepseek-v4.1-flash` reasoned, said "Sorry, I can't respond to this
question.", and ended with `finish_reason: "content_filter"` and no output
tokens, all under a 200 (#540). Since 0.2.4 that line is taken out of a
streamed chat ending `content_filter`, so the reply says nothing before the
filter's stop: magpie hands such a refusal to the group's next member
instead of passing it to the agent as an answer. Only text that is still
the filter's line is held, so any other reply's words go as they come; the
same words ending `stop`, or the filter cutting off a reply after other
words, go through as they came.
copilot.tencent.com sends the line with a newline on each side
(`"\nSorry, I can't respond to this question.\n"`); since 0.2.5 white
space around it no longer lets it through. It also puts `"tool_calls": []` on
every delta; since 0.2.6 only a list with a call in it lets the reply
through as it came.

## Models

When you are signed in, the models are the ones WorkBuddy's product config
gives its CLI agent (`GET /v3/config`), with their context, image input and
reasoning levels. Until then, or if WorkBuddy doesn't answer, the list below
is used.

`workbuddy`:
- Auto
- Hy4 preview, Hy3, Hy3-X
- Deepseek-V4.1-Flash, Deepseek-V4-Pro
- GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3-Flash, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.1, GLM-5v-Turbo
- MiniMax-M3
- Kimi-K3, Kimi-K2.7-Code, Kimi-K2.6

`workbuddy-ai`:
- Default, Fast, Balanced, Primary, Deep
- GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.3-Codex
- Gemini-3.1-Pro, Gemini-3.5-Flash
- GLM-5.3, GLM-5.2
- Hy3
- Kimi-K3, Kimi-K2.6
- MiniMax-M3

A model's reasoning levels are its variants (`reasoningEffort`). A chat
that names no level goes at the model's own default from the config
(`reasoning.defaultEffort`, "high" for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), as WorkBuddy's
client sends it: WorkBuddy doesn't think when a chat names none, so
OpenCode's default variant got answers without thinking. An effort the
client names, `none` too, goes as it came.

Two values differ from the config, each measured with real requests:

- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (and its paid `-sg` id) lists `none`, though the
  config says it only reasons: WorkBuddy answers `reasoning_effort: "none"`
  on it with no thinking at all (since 0.2.7, #563).
- On `workbuddy` (copilot.tencent.com), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's context is
  100000, not the config's 1000000: a longer prompt is refused with
  "prompt is too long: … > 100000 maximum", while GLM-5.3-Flash on the same
  endpoint takes the million. `workbuddy-ai` takes the million on it
  (since 0.2.7, #561).

A chat goes gzipped (`Content-Encoding: gzip`), as WorkBuddy's own client
sends its model requests (`RequestBodyGzip` in both builds' product.json).
Claude's Messages route goes as it came, and so does anything that isn't a
chat completion: magpie's drawings (`/v2/images/generations`,
`/v2/images/edits`) go as plain JSON, which is all the images API reads.

A model's price is its `credits` ("x0.29") and the config's
`modelPromotions`. A discount for whole days (Step-5-Preview's 独家限免) is
the price now, with the price before it (`rateWas`). A price that holds only
some hours of the day (Hy4 preview, free 23:00–8:00) is given as its full
price, never as free: magpie keeps the list until it asks again, so a list
asked for at night would say "free" all day (#121).

### Free models only

Each site (WorkBuddy, WorkBuddy AI) has a "Free models only" switch in its
provider settings in magpie, off by default (#430). When it is on:

- the list holds only the models the site serves at no cost now. A model free
  only at night, or one with no price, counts as paid;
- a request for any other model is answered by the plugin with a 404
  `model_not_found` and never sent, so no credits are spent. magpie rests
  only that model and tries the next provider;
- if the price list can't be read, nothing is sent (503), since whether the
  model is free is unknown. An API key WorkBuddy lists no prices for lists
  no models.

The price list is read again at most once a minute for requests.

## Credits in magpie

magpie's usage card shows the account's credits from the resource summary.
It also says when the soonest credits left run out (`runsOutAt`, and how
many: `runsOut`), from the paid and free package lists WorkBuddy's own
client reads. The daily Free Plan slice isn't counted: it ends at the same
midnight on every account. magpie's smart routing spends the account whose
credits run out first.

An enterprise (team) account's resource summary lists no packages. Its
credits are read from the enterprise meter
(`/billing/meter/get-enterprise-user-usage`), the one WorkBuddy's own usage
page reads: the cycle's credits used of its limit, and when the cycle
resets (magpie #1904).

## The free model's daily window (WorkBuddy AI)

The credits above are not the only limit. `deepseek-v4.1-flash` is served at
`x0.00` and costs the plan nothing, yet WorkBuddy AI refuses it long before
160 credits are touched:

```
429 usage exceeds frequency limit, but don't worry, your usage will reset at
2026-10-20 19:47:41 UTC+8, alternatively, you can switch to the other models
to continue using it.
```

That is a token allowance of its own — per account, per 24 hours, about 1e8
tokens, counted as prompt + cache-read + completion. Nothing the vendor
answers with reports it, so the plugin rebuilds the current window from
magpie's `usage.jsonl` and gives it to the card as **Free model tokens**
beside **Credits**. `quota alert` and `magpie quota` show it too; before,
the card read 0% on an account that was already refused.

What is measured, and what is easy to read wrongly:

- **`cache_read` counts.** Prompt and completion alone are 20× smaller and
  never approach the cap, so a window read that way looks empty while full.
- **The window is fixed, not sliding.** It runs 24 hours from the first
  request answered after the previous window ended, not from the reset
  instant; a gap between the two means the new window starts later.
- **`deepseek-v4.1-flash-sg` shares the window.** It is the paid id of the
  same model (`ModelRateLimitCap` in the product config), not a second
  allowance — switching to it continues the same window, at `x0.03`.
- **1e8 is an estimate within 0.2%.** The largest value seen to still be
  answered is 100,183,315, and the next request is refused, so it cannot be
  probed higher.
- **A refusal is exact, and the sum is not.** The ledger is this machine's
  only: one window was refused at 92,792,962 because the rest of that
  account's spending happened on another machine, which read as 93%. So a
  429 whose named reset is still ahead makes the window full — `used: 100`,
  `resetsAt` the reset the vendor named — whatever the rows add up to. The
  sum carries the window only until the first refusal.
- **The card names both ids**, `deepseek-v4.1-flash` and
  `deepseek-v4.1-flash-sg`: magpie matches a window's models by exact id
  (only an `@size` suffix folds into the bare id), so one alone would leave
  the other unrestricted.
- **The ledger is read in magpie's own folder** (`appdir.Config()`: the
  portable data folder, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/magpie` when that is set (an
  absolute path, as `appdir.rooted` has it), or `~/.config/magpie`), from its
  end backwards — a heavy ledger runs to hundreds of MB.
  - The window is a chain, so where it now began depends on every window
    before it: read a slice of the ledger that starts mid-chain and every
    window after it is shifted (4% on an account two hours from its cap, or
    100% on one still served). The read therefore goes back until it reaches
    an edge this account's own rows spell out — a refusal whose reset can be
    read, or a gap of a day between two of its answered rows — plus a day
    below that, and with neither it reads to the file's start, where there is
    no earlier window to be shifted by.
  - Nothing bounds that by age, so two things keep a heavy ledger cheap: a
    line's time is read before the line is decoded, so a line under the edge
    (of any provider or account) ends the read at once; and a read past 24h
    with no answered free-model row of this account stops, since the window
    has lapsed and nothing would be reported. Both bounds leave out a line
    a client reported (`"source":"reported"`, #1874): magpie appends those
    dated where the client's call happened, so a backfilled row says nothing
    about where the file has got to.
  - `providerAccount` is the account's label. Two accounts sharing a label
    get its slot added (`pluginLabels`), the label no longer matches what
    their rows were written under, and the card reports no free window.
- **The offset comes from the refusal's words** (`UTC+8`, `GMT-5`,
  `UTC+05:30`). A reset whose offset cannot be read is no edge at all,
  rather than +08:00 guessed.

A window that has lapsed reports nothing rather than 0%: nothing is
exhausted, and the next request opens a fresh one. The China build is not
covered; its limit has not been measured.

## When free models work but a credit model does not

Check the failing account and model separately before concluding that the
wallet is empty:

- Use the exact API id from the account's model list. For example,
  `glm-5.3-flash` is the id; `GLM-5.3-Flash` is its display name. A route
  copied from another provider need not be a valid WorkBuddy model id.
- The WorkBuddy 5.6+ encrypted-desktop message means this sign-in cannot
  be read, not that the account has zero credits. Use **Account (browser)**
  for the same build/region. Keep the old entry until the new identity and
  model list are confirmed. The desktop file is not decrypted or changed.
- An account restricted by WorkBuddy is a different failure. Code 11140
  with its unusual-activity message calls for **Submit feedback** in
  WorkBuddy; signing in repeatedly or changing the model does not lift it.
  See [magpie#1849](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/issues/1849).
- Inspect each attempted provider/account in magpie's routing details.
  A ZCode trial quota failure, another provider's insufficient credits, or
  one account's restriction is not the balance of every WorkBuddy account.

A model response confirms that the selected account can answer. It does
not, without a matching vendor usage record, prove how many credits that
request deducted. A usage-read error means the balance is unknown.

The encrypted-desktop result can be reproduced without an account using
`packages/workbuddy/usage.test.mjs` in an isolated temporary HOME (and
USERPROFILE on Windows). It covers sign-in, usage and chat against a
synthetic sealed desktop file, and checks that the file stays unchanged.
A successful browser authorization alone is not a migration: compare the
returned identity with the intended desktop account before replacing its
entry. An already signed-in browser can simply renew another saved account.


## Not here

magpie's built-in WorkBuddy does more than this package: several accounts
under one provider.

OpenCode's plugin API has no place for these.

Credit multipliers accept the international catalog's `x0.34 credits` text as well as `x0.34`. An empty credits value (for example Auto) stays unknown, never free.

## Daily check-in

The account's daily credits are claimed through the billing meter. magpie
can run it once a day per account when its WorkBuddy check-in switch is on;
Settings → Usage → Plugins has that switch and a *Check in now* button.
The activity status is read first: inactive is `inactive`, a day already
checked in is `done`, and only an active unchecked day is claimed. A claim
that WorkBuddy answers 1001, 1002 or 1003 is `done`, `ineligible` or
`inactive`. A claim turned away 401 while the account's credits still read
is `ineligible`: that check-in takes WorkBuddy's own app. A transient
billing failure is retried twice before the card shows the failure.
Only WorkBuddy (China) checks in: the AI build has no claim endpoint, and
its plugin carries no check-in hook.
A request that gets no answer at all leaves the hook as a thrown error, so
magpie retries it on its 1-minute offline backoff rather than the 30-minute
one it gives a failed answer (#149).

An `inactive` answer is kept for the whole Beijing day: the plugin host
gives it no recheck, and a manual refresh reads the kept one (tracked in
[yetone/magpie#2696](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/issues/2696)).

@magpie-community/opencode-zcode-auth.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-zcode-auth

Signs in to Z.ai's GLM Coding Plan, or BigModel's (智谱). It does this the
way [ZCode](https://zcode.z.ai) does, and serves the plan's GLM models
over Anthropic's Messages API. Provider id: `zcode`.

## Signing in

- **ZCode: Z.ai GLM Coding Plan** and **ZCode: BigModel (智谱) GLM Coding Plan**
  - zcode.z.ai opens a sign-in flow, and the browser signs in to Z.ai or to
    BigModel. The plugin polls the flow until it is done, so there is
    nothing to paste.
  - With that sign-in it takes the key named `zcode-api-key` from the
    account's default project, or makes it if it isn't there, as ZCode does.
    Requests go to `api.z.ai/api/anthropic` or
    `open.bigmodel.cn/api/anthropic`.
  - If the account has no plan of its own, it looks for a seat on a team's
    plan and uses that team project's `zcode-team-api-key`.
  - Failing both, it uses ZCode's free **Start Plan**, served by zcode.z.ai
    with ZCode's session token.
  - zcode.z.ai serves the Start Plan only to requests that look like the
    ZCode client's own, and refuses others with HTTP 405 "request has been
    blocked due to unusual activity". So a Start Plan request goes as
    ZCode's does: ZCode's headers, ZCode's three system blocks with the
    agent's system prompt at the end of the third (a fourth block is
    refused, #343), the day in a `<system-reminder>` turn before the agent's
    turns, and the sign-in's device id in `metadata.user_id`. GLM Coding
    Plan and team requests go as the agent sent them, but for that same
    `metadata.user_id` when the agent sent none: ZCode puts it on every
    request, and the plan's endpoint keeps a prompt cache on the machine it
    picks by it, so without it the cache is mostly missed (#387). An
    account known only by its key gets a device id made from the key, the
    same on every start. Every request also carries the `x-session-id`
    header below. zcode.z.ai also
    answers 405 code 3012 to every request of an account its risk control
    blocked, ZCode's own app's included (plugins#348). That answer comes
    back as ZCode's words, then "ZCode's risk control blocked this account
    for unusual activity (code 3012); …", which magpie reads as the account
    restricted: it rests, and the group's other providers are used. Only
    ZCode support lifts such a block. A block page from ZCode's edge
    firewall says this network's address was blocked instead.
  - The Start Plan's token can't be refreshed. When it runs out, sign in
    again.
  - Every request, on any plan, names its conversation in `x-session-id`,
    as ZCode does: a bare UUID, the same on each turn. BigModel's prompt
    cache follows it: without it a long conversation's turns hit the cache
    about one time in twenty, with it nearly every turn (#387). The
    agent's own session id (magpie tells it to the plugin) goes as it is
    when it is a UUID, else as a UUID made from it, so the vendor sees
    only ZCode's format; with none, a UUID made from the device. The same
    id is `metadata.user_id`'s `session_id`, as in ZCode's requests.
- **ZCode: a team's GLM Coding Plan**
  - For an account with a plan of its own and a seat on a team's plan
    (#285). The sign-ins above take the account's own plan, as ZCode does
    by default; this one asks which site, signs in the same way, and
    takes the team seat's `zcode-team-api-key`, as ZCode does when its
    plan picker is switched to the team's plan.
  - It is kept as an account of its own, named `<email> (team)`, beside
    the account's own plan, so both can be used.
  - With no seat on a team's plan, it says so and signs in to nothing.
  - The same ZCode session also reads the person's gift plans. Their
    `<model>-Trial` entries and gift buckets appear beside the team's
    models and allowance. Plain models spend the team plan; trial entries
    spend the personal gift, with no fallback to the team on refusal.
- **ZCode app's sign-in**
  - Uses the account the ZCode app on this computer is signed in to. For
    every request it reads ZCode's own credentials (`~/.zcode/v2`), so it
    follows ZCode as it signs in again, renews its session or switches to a
    team's plan, but only while ZCode is signed in to that same account.
    Once ZCode signs out, or signs in to another account, the sign-in uses
    what it saved when it was added; when that session has run out, it
    asks to be signed in again. It never sends one account's requests with
    another's credentials: to use both, add the app's sign-in once for each.
- **GLM Coding Plan API key**
  - Paste a key (`<id>.<secret>`) and say which site it is from.
  - A key reaches the GLM Coding Plan alone. ZCode's gift plans (the
    Start Plan, ZCode 1024 Dev Day) are served to ZCode's own session,
    which a key doesn't carry: for an account with only a gift plan, the
    card and each refused request (1113) say to sign in with ZCode
    instead. For an account with a GLM Coding Plan, the card says the
    gift plans' `-Trial` models need ZCode's sign-in, since a key lists
    none of them.

## Where the sign-in is kept

In OpenCode's `auth.json` (magpie: `plugin-auth.json`), under `zcode`:

- **The browser sign-ins** are kept as an `oauth` entry:
  - `access` is the key.
  - `refresh` is JSON holding the site, the endpoint, the key, ZCode's
    token, the team project, the plan and a device id of this plugin's own.
- **A pasted key** is kept as an `api` entry, with the site in `metadata`.

The plugin never writes ZCode's own credential store. It reads it only for
the ZCode app's sign-in (`refresh` then holds `"source": "zcode"`).

## How requests are routed

Before each request, the plugin checks which plan the account is on, and
asks again every 10 minutes, and with every read of the usage card, so a
plan bought, a gift claimed or a plan lapsed reaches the requests when the
card shows it. A key whose plan list once reads no plan after reading one
is asked again after a minute, and a Start Plan refusal on such a key reads
the plans again on the next request:

- If the key's account has a GLM Coding Plan
  (`/api/biz/subscription/list`), its requests go to that plan. A model
  the account's gift plans also serve is listed again as
  `<model>-Trial`; asking that entry spends the gift (see below).
- Otherwise they go to the gift plans.

Every request carries the key as both `x-api-key` and
`Authorization: Bearer`.

**The gift's trial entries.** An account with a GLM Coding Plan can
also hold gift plans from ZCode activities, ones that expire on a fixed
date. Their allowance would lapse unused if every request went to the
coding plan, so the plugin reads the gift's balance (per the sign-in's
session, kept for 10 minutes) and lists every model a live bucket
serves again as `<model>-Trial`, named in the catalog's spelling
(GLM-5.3-Flash-Trial). Asking a trial entry sends the model to the
gift, dressed as ZCode's own; asking the plain model spends the coding
plan — the choice is the user's. A bucket is judged spent only by its
`remaining_units` — a missing one is unknown, not spent. A trial entry
whose bucket is spent or blocked answers 429 without touching the
coding plan; when the gift answers a trial entry with a quota error
(code 1113 "Insufficient balance or no resource package", code 1005
"exceed quota limit", which it can answer inside an HTTP 200) that too
becomes a 429 and keeps the entry off for a minute. Any other gift
answer (its 405, its 401, its 5xx) goes on as it came: the user picked
the gift, so the coding plan is not spent behind their back. Every other
429 counts as spent — Z.ai's 1302/1303 rate limits among them — while the
plan's own in-flight cap (3008/3009) does not: such a request is asked
again instead (see [A few at once](#a-few-at-once)). A stream's body is
never read or buffered on the way.

**Free first.** Picking `-Trial` by hand keeps the choice the user's,
but an agent that always asks the plain model never sees the gift.
`freeFirst` turns the preference around: the plain model spends the
account's own live gift first, and falls back to the coding plan when
the gift cannot serve it — a bucket that is spent, a model the gift
does not serve, no ZCode session, or the minute's rest a refusal just
earned. Turn it on for the whole plugin in magpie's Plugins › Options

```json
{ "freeFirst": true }
```

or on the provider alone, under `provider.zcode.options` in the config
magpie hands its plugins — a key only `plugins.json`'s `config` carries,
so the plugin's own options are the ones magpie's Plugins › Options
edits. Where both say something, the provider's word stands. An account
with a coding plan and a gift spends the gift until it is spent, then
the plan; a gift-only account already goes to the gift by its plain
names, so the option changes nothing there. Across the accounts magpie
rotates, each spends its own gift before its own plan — which is the
point: free allowance is spent before subscribed quota, on every
account, with no per-account naming to keep up.

Two boundaries worth knowing. The gift is judged before the request is
sent, from the balance read the plugin keeps for ten minutes: a gift
that runs out between that read and the send has its refusal answered
from the plan in the same request — any gift failure is, its own
waited-out busy cap included, and the replay waits out the plan's busy
cap as any plan request does — and a spent answer or a block page rests
the model a minute and drops the route's balance read, so the requests
behind it go straight to the plan. A gift that cannot be asked at all —
the network, the host — is answered from the plan the same way, the
route read dropped for the next request, while a caller's own abort
stays an abort. The agent sees the plan's answer
either way. And the `-Trial` entries keep their own strict semantics —
asking one is still an explicit pick of the gift alone, never the plan;
a spent one answers 429 with freeFirst on, as it does without it.

## A few at once

A plan serves one account a few requests at a time; past that, ZCode
answers 429 with code 3008 "user concurrency limit exceeded", or 3009
"model concurrency limit exceeded". magpie funnels every agent's and every
session's requests of one computer through this one plugin process, so
magpie's own queue spaces an account's requests by the number this plugin
declares — `maxConcurrency` on the auth hook, and `magpie.maxConcurrency`
in its `package.json`, both three. A request the vendor refuses anyway
waits a moment (a quarter of a second, then longer — about ten seconds of
waits in all) and asks again, the same request byte for byte. A cap that
outlasts the waits goes on as a 429, ZCode's words followed by what they
mean, so the agent reads why. magpie still reads it as a rate limit: the
account rests a minute and the request goes to the next member of its
routing group, as it did before.

Three is a default, not a cap the plugin enforces. A plan's real cap
follows its tier — Z.ai serves a Max plan more at once than a Pro, and a
Lite fewer — and is higher off-peak
([Z.ai's usage policy](https://docs.z.ai/devpack/usage-policy)), so a
number written into the plugin would hold a Max account to a Lite one's
with no way to raise it. A user who knows their plan's cap sets it on the
account or the provider in magpie, and magpie's queue follows that.

## The usage card

An account with both plans shows both allowances: the coding plan's
windows first, then the gift's buckets, each with its own name, models
and end. The card's plan and term stay the coding plan's. A gift read
that fails leaves just the coding card — magpie hides a card's windows
behind an error, so a gift hiccup must not black out a working Coding
Plan. A gift that goes out of date while requests use it simply stops
showing. Beside the coding plan's windows each gift bucket is named by
its model first, as ZCode's own "Today's balance" lists it, then by its
plan ("GLM-5.1-Trial · Start Plan"), one plan or several, so the two
allowances can't be read as one. The model comes first because magpie's
ring and account row cut a long name short: "ZCODE GLOBAL BUI…" (the
Start Plan claimed on 10-29) said neither (#504).

**Gift plans that start later.** A plan on the balance whose `starts_at`
is still to come (a Start Plan taking effect at 23:00 today) serves
nothing yet: no request goes to it and its buckets don't count. The card
names it in a line set aside, "ZCode gift plan not started yet", with
the plan's name and its start in this computer's time as the display
("Start Plan · 2026-10-29 23:00"), soonest first. An account whose only
gift plan starts later gets a card with that line, not "ended or never
started". The status ZCode gives such a plan has not been seen, so any
status but `expired` is taken; `starts_at` decides it.

**Resets.** A GLM Coding Plan of the account's own, and a team seat,
show the resets the vendor's usage page lists
(`/api/biz/customer-package-reset/list`, `targetType=PERSONAL` with the
plan's key, `TEAM` with the team's sign-in): how many of the five hours
and of the week are still available, and when each runs out, soonest
first. A team's are marked a team's. They are only read; a reset is
spent on the vendor's own page. A list that can't be read, or has none
left, shows no count.

**Gift plans ZCode holds but has not granted.** ZCode hands out one-off
trust-build / gift plans (a day's ZCode Trust Build, say) that are not
on the account until the ZCode app claims them. The plugin reads the
app's own lists of them with the card and names them there: its claim
banners' feed (`GET /api/v1/marketing/touch`, each delivery's
`claim_zcode_plan` button) and `GET /api/v1/zcode-plan/billing/preview`.
A banner plan (a weekend's ZCODE WEEKEND BUILD, 10-30) is in the feed
alone, never in the preview (#503) — the window is named "Gift plans to
claim in the ZCode app" and the display shows "1 · ZCode Trust Build"
— set aside, so the line stops nothing and routing, usage caps and the
menu bar pass it over. The name is a fixed sentence magpie can
translate; the count and the plan's own name are the display. Reading
the card never claims one. A preview that fails, or lists nothing, adds
no line at all, and a card that is an error keeps its error. Claim the
plan in the ZCode app (open it once), or let the daily claim below do it;
the next read shows it as an ordinary gift bucket.

## The daily claim

With ZCode turned on in magpie's Settings → Daily check-in (it is off
until you turn it on), magpie has the plugin claim each account's gift
plans once a day (`auth.checkin`; `magpie accounts checkin` asks now). It
reads both lists above (the banners' feed and the preview, each plan
once) and posts each plan to
`POST /api/v1/zcode-plan/billing/claim` (`{"plan_id": …}`) with the
account's ZCode session, as the app does. The answer is judged by the
body's code, not the HTTP status:

- nothing listed: *inactive* (ZCode answers an account with nothing to
  claim `{"code":0,"msg":""}`, with no list at all). A list that doesn't
  read is *failed*, never nothing to claim. A plan just claimed may show
  in neither `billing/preview` nor `billing/current` until its
  `effective_at`, so neither list is read as "claimed or not";
- code 0: *claimed* (the next request uses the plan);
- code 1003 "target already exists" (HTTP 200): *done*, claimed before;
- code 3007 "captcha verify failed": *captcha*, the plan is claimed in
  the ZCode app (on 10-06 ZCode wanted the app's Aliyun captcha for a
  claim; whether it still does for a fresh plan is not known yet);
- anything else, an HTTP error without a code, or a reply that isn't
  JSON: *failed*, which magpie asks again later that day. It is never
  taken as claimed, and a failed claim leaves the account's sign-in
  alone.

An account added with a GLM Coding Plan key has no ZCode session to claim
with (*ineligible*).

**No ZCode session.** A card read with a key, or with a sign-in whose
ZCode session has run out (it can't be renewed), sets aside a line named
"ZCode gift plans (-Trial models) need ZCode's sign-in", with why in its
display: such an account reads no gift and lists no `-Trial` entries.
Sign in again with ZCode to get them back. A gift read that fails
otherwise is asked again a minute later, not ten.

## Models

The models are the ones ZCode offers for the account's plan. They come
from ZCode's provider config: the release zcode.z.ai names, or an
installed ZCode's copy if that one is newer. The list is kept for 10
minutes. When the config can't be read, the plugin falls back to this list
(and magpie keeps the list it was told last, unless the account's gift
plans add `-Trial` entries, which are told as read):

| Model | Context | Output | Efforts |
|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3 | 1M | 128K | low, high, max |
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 1M | 128K | low, high, max |
| GLM-5.2 | 1M | 128K | none, high, max |
| GLM-5-Turbo | 200K | 64K | none, high |

The Start Plan's config has all of these except GLM-5.3. An account
with no GLM Coding Plan also lists every model its gift plans serve under
the model's own name, as ZCode does (the Start Plan's GLM-5.3 bucket makes
GLM-5.3 a model), since all of its requests go to the gift anyway.

A gift plan's models appear again as `<model>-Trial` entries, so a
request can spend the gift's quota on purpose. A trial entry is listed
while any live bucket serves its model, spent buckets included (a spent
entry answers 429 rather than vanishing mid-session).

Two plans can give one model (ZCode Trust Build and the Start Plan both
give GLM-5.3-Flash). The server picks the bucket, so the usage card
counts the model on its live bucket, the least used, and sets a spent
sibling aside. A spent sibling never makes the model, or the account,
look used up while another bucket still has quota.

@magpie-community/opencode-zed-auth.readme:
# @magpie-community/opencode-zed-auth

Signs in to a **Zed** subscription (Zed Pro, its trial, a student or business
plan) and calls the models Zed hosts: Anthropic's, OpenAI's, Google's and
xAI's, through `cloud.zed.dev`, the way the Zed editor calls them. Provider
id: `zed`. Ported from magpie's built-in Zed account.

## Sign-in

**Sign in with Zed (browser)** is Zed's own sign-in:

1. The plugin makes an RSA-2048 key and listens on a port of `127.0.0.1`.
2. The browser opens `zed.dev/native_app_signin` with that port and the
   key's public half.
3. Once you sign in, zed.dev sends the browser back to the port with your
   user id and an access token encrypted to the key. The browser is then
   sent on to zed.dev's "signed in" page.
4. The plugin asks Zed who the account is (`/client/users/me`). That gives
   the organization the models are called under, and its plan. An
   organization with Zed's hosted models turned off is refused.

## Organization

Zed asks for a model token per organization. The Zed editor starts in the
account's default organization and lets you switch to another from its
title bar. The plugin has no switcher, so it picks the organization with a
plan that calls models (any plan but Free), in this order (#232):

1. the organization it saved before, while that one still has such a plan;
2. the default organization, if it has one;
3. the personal organization, if it has one;
4. any other organization that has one.

When none has such a plan, it keeps what Zed picks: the saved organization,
else the default, else the first. The plan shown is the picked
organization's own (none when Zed lists none for it), never the account's
plan in its place. When Zed answers 402 for the organization a sign-in was
saved under ("Organization does not have an active subscription"), the
plugin reads the account again, moves to an organization with a plan if
there is one, saves it with the sign-in, and asks once more. The plan card
re-checks the organization the same way.

The sign-in is kept as an `oauth` entry: `access` is the access token and
`refresh` is JSON holding the user id, machine id, organization and plan.
Zed has no refresh token, so the token lasts until Zed refuses it. When
Zed refuses it, you are asked to sign in again. `accountId` is the account's
GitHub login.

## Requests

- **Model token:** each request uses a short-lived model token, minted from
  the sign-in with `POST /client/llm_tokens` and kept in memory. If Zed calls
  the token stale (a 401, `x-zed-expired-token` or `x-zed-outdated-token`),
  it is minted again once.
- **API per model:** each model is declared on the AI SDK package of its
  own provider, so the request the SDK writes is already what Zed wants.
  The plugin's `fetch` wraps it as `{provider, model, provider_request}` and
  sends it to `POST /completions` with Zed's headers:

  | Zed provider | AI SDK package | API |
  |---|---|---|
  | anthropic | `@ai-sdk/anthropic` | Messages |
  | open_ai | `@ai-sdk/openai` | Responses |
  | x_ai | `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` | chat completions |
  | google | `@ai-sdk/google` | generateContent |

- **Request changes, as magpie makes them:**
  - Anthropic: the request loses `stream`, since the cloud always streams.
    Every `tool_result` gets `is_error` (Zed's cloud refuses one without it).
  - xAI: `max_tokens` becomes `max_completion_tokens`.
  - Gemini: the model is named in the request as `models/<id>`.
- **Replies:**
  - Zed's newline-delimited lines are sent back as each API's own
    server-sent events.
  - A caller that didn't ask for a stream gets one whole reply.
  - A failure Zed reports mid-stream keeps its status (429, 402, 529 …).
    So does a reply without Zed's `stream_ended`, which comes back as an
    error rather than a shorter answer, except one case. A streamed xAI
    (chat) reply that has already said something, and has no tool call
    half written, ends cut short instead, with a note saying so, a `stop`
    and `[DONE]` (#91). magpie's gateway can go on with an Anthropic or
    Responses reply cut short, but not with a chat one.
  - A 402 means the plan doesn't include Zed's hosted models, or its
    allowance is used up.

## Models

- **After sign-in:** the account's own list comes from Zed's `GET /models`,
  read when you sign in and every 10 minutes after. Disabled models are
  left out. Each model's effort levels become its variants. When a read
  fails, the list read last is kept; when none was ever read (Zed down,
  or a list with nothing callable, as for an organization without an
  active subscription), the hook throws why, and magpie shows that reason
  with the account, the declared models marked as not its list (#229).
- **Before sign-in:** the config hook declares one model of each family
  (Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 5.5, Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash,
  Grok 4.7), which the account's list replaces.

## Usage

magpie's `auth.usage` hook shows what Zed tells its editor of the plan,
as magpie's built-in Zed account did. Zed doesn't report how much of the
allowance is spent, so there are no windows:

- the plan's name (Pro, Pro Trial, Business, Student, VIP). A free
  account's card says "No plan"; its account row still names it Free;
- when the billing period ends;
- an overdue invoice, as the card's error ("its models are paused");
- a sign-in Zed refuses (`/users/me` or the model list answering 401)
  marks the account as needing to sign in again. A plan that changed is
  saved with the sign-in.

## In magpie, not the plugin

These come from magpie itself, as they did for the built-in:

- Several Zed accounts at once. magpie keeps a sign-in per account and
  switches between them; plain OpenCode keeps one sign-in per provider.
- Web search. A model that can't search is given magpie's web-search
  stand-in, when a search API is set up in magpie.

@magpie-community/opencode-zen-free-auth.readme:
# OpenCode Zen Free

OpenCode Zen's free models in magpie and OpenCode. Provider id:
`opencode-zen-free`.

Since 2026-10-13 Zen's free tier answers 403 FreeTierError ("can only be
used from within OpenCode") to a request that isn't OpenCode's. From
0.1.6 the plugin sends a free-model request with exactly the headers
OpenCode sends to Zen, and a session id of OpenCode's own form. Older
versions (0.1.1 on npm before it) get the 403: update the plugin.

Since 2026-10-26 Zen's free tier answers `429 FreeUsageLimitError`
("Free models work in OpenCode") to the User-Agent OpenCode 1.19.0 sent,
which 0.1.6 to 0.1.15 sent on every request. From 0.1.16 the plugin
sends OpenCode 2.0.25's headers (`opencode/latest/2.0.25/cli`, its
session id under `x-session-affinity` and `x-session-id` too): update
the plugin.

## Install

```sh
magpie plugin add @magpie-community/opencode-zen-free-auth
magpie plugin login opencode-zen-free
```

## Sign in

Enter `public` in the key field. No personal API key is needed.

Hosts supporting magpie's `keyless` and `single` auth metadata can enable
this public identity without a key field and offer Sign in again instead
of another account. Older hosts and OpenCode keep the public-key flow.
Personal keys still belong to the built-in OpenCode Zen provider.

Whatever is typed in the key field, the plugin signs in with the one
shared `public` credential: a key made under your own OpenCode account
does nothing here, and several of them don't make several accounts. Your
own Zen keys go in magpie's built-in OpenCode Zen provider (or OpenCode's
`opencode` provider), which takes several keys.
The credential is kept in OpenCode's `auth.json` or magpie's
`plugin-auth.json`.

## Models

The plugin discovers Zen's current free models, including their context
windows and reasoning levels. Use `opencode-zen-free/<model>`, for example
`opencode-zen-free/big-pickle`.

Retired models and SystemOne models are excluded. The list is asked
again each time the host lists models (magpie does this on start and every
hour): a model Zen no longer gives free leaves it, and a new free one joins
it. A model Zen lists as `-free` that OpenCode's catalog and docs don't
describe yet (or can't be read) is offered too, on Chat Completions, as
OpenCode asks a model with no package of its own. When Zen's list can't be
read, the last list is kept. A request for a
model that isn't free now gets a 404 naming the free ones; one made free
since the last list is served after the list is asked again (at most once a
minute). Availability and rate limits are set by Zen; the plugin has no
remaining-quota data.

## Requests

Requests go to `https://opencode.ai/inference/v1` using each model's native
Chat Completions, Responses or Anthropic Messages API. Streaming and
ordinary JSON replies are supported.

The agent's tools are preserved. Zen's models often call OpenCode's own
tool names; such a call is given the agent's tool whose name differs only
in case (`bash` to `Bash`), or else only in case and `_`/`-` (`todowrite`
to `todo_write`, `webfetch` to `web_fetch`), when exactly one does. A
call of a tool the agent has no spelling of (`psh` beside `pwsh`, `bedit`)
reaches the agent as the model called it, as with any other provider: the
agent answers it with its own unknown-tool error, and the model corrects
the name and goes on. Only a call with no name is left out, and the
reply's text says so; a turn whose every call was left out ends as an
ordinary answer. Tools run in the agent.

Zen's free tier only answers a request that carries tools, so a request
is sent with the five core OpenCode tools the agent doesn't declare
itself (`bash`, `edit`, `glob`, `grep`, `read`), described as not
available. A call of one of them the agent doesn't have reaches the agent
like any other.

Zen's free tier also tells OpenCode's own requests by the environment
block every OpenCode prompt ends with (`<env>`, a `Working directory:`
line, `</env>`) in a system message. Another agent's request without one
gets a small allowance a day and then `429 FreeUsageLimitError` ("Free
models work in OpenCode") until 00:00 UTC, while OpenCode's go through.
So a request whose system messages have no such block gets one added
after the agent's own prompt (Anthropic `system` and Responses
`instructions` likewise); a prompt that has one, as OpenCode's does, goes
as it is. The block added is OpenCode's own, with the working directory
the agent's prompt names (Codex's `<cwd>`, a `Working directory:` line,
"the current working directory is ...") or the user's home folder when it
names none. A fixed placeholder there is refused: since 2026-10-29 Zen
answers `Working directory: unknown`, which 0.1.15 to 0.1.17 sent, with
that 429 at once.

Now and then Zen closes a streamed Chat Completions reply before its
`[DONE]`. When the reply has said something and no tool call of it is
unfinished, it ends there as an ordinary answer, and its text says it was
cut short; asking again goes on. A reply cut short with a tool call
unfinished, with nothing said, or collapsed for a client that doesn't
stream fails with an error naming the reply's id and how much of it came.
An Anthropic Messages or Responses reply cut short fails too: magpie
tells it from a whole one and, where the model can, goes on with it.

manifest.description: 在 magpie 窗口里加一个「Agent 控制台」页面：用常驻本地服务驱动本机的 Agent CLI（Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 等），带结构化时间线。A Magpie page that drives local Agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and others) with a persistent local daemon and a structured timeline.
manifest.author: qingnian108 (https://github.com/qingnian108)

@magpie-community/page-agent-console.readme:
# Agent Console

A Magpie page plugin that drives real local Agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Devin, dsh). Each conversation is a **persistent Agent session** on a standalone Node daemon. Close or refresh the page — the Agent keeps running while Magpie is open. Reopen the page and you pick up where you left off. When Magpie quits, the daemon and its Agents stop; threads are persisted and can be resumed next time.

## Install

Requires [Magpie](https://usemagpie.ai) ≥ 0.1.1340 and Node.js ≥ 20.

```bash
magpie plugin add @magpie-community/page-agent-console
```

Or in Magpie: **Settings → Plugins → Add plugin**, enter `@magpie-community/page-agent-console` (or find **Agent Console** in Discover). After install, **Agent Console** appears in the sidebar plugin group.

Install the Agent CLIs you want to use (for example `claude` or `codex`). Missing CLIs show an install hint in Settings.

A cold install is about **46 MB** of `node_modules`, mostly `node-pty`'s native terminal module (~26 MB). Claude Code is **not** bundled: to use the Claude Code Agent, install the `claude` CLI yourself (`npm i -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` or Anthropic's native installer). / 冷安装约占 **46 MB** 的 `node_modules`，主要是 `node-pty` 原生终端模块（约 26 MB）。插件**不**附带 Claude Code：要用 Claude Code Agent，请自行安装 `claude` CLI（`npm i -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` 或 Anthropic 的原生安装器）。

---

This is not a gateway chat box. The daemon talks to the real CLIs through `claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json` (the user's own `claude`, with its control messages for permissions, interrupt, model and mode), `codex app-server`, and ACP, normalizes a structured event stream (tool calls, thinking, permission requests, usage), and pushes it to the React page over WebSocket.

UI principle: **obvious at a glance, nothing extra**. Three columns — sidebar (projects × threads), conversation timeline, and a right panel (changes / files / terminal).

## Features

- **Persistent sessions**: each thread binds to a long-lived Agent process; after a daemon restart, running threads are marked closed and can be resumed (`--resume` / `thread/resume`)
- **Multiple Agents**: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Devin, dsh; missing CLIs show an install hint
- **Model / permission / thinking**: per-thread; four permission modes and five thinking levels (what each Agent actually supports)
- **Structured timeline**: user message → thinking (expandable) → tool calls (read / edit / command, with line-level diffs) → todos → usage and duration; answer permission requests (tools / plan / questions) on the card
- **Steer and queue**: steer while running, queue the next message, interrupt
- **Changes panel**: git status refresh every 3s, unified per-file diffs; discarded untracked files go to trash instead of a hard delete
- **Files panel**: lazy directory tree (respects `.gitignore`), syntax-highlighted preview
- **Terminal panel**: real PTY via node-pty (pwsh / powershell); reconnects after reopening the page; degrades if PTY is unavailable
- **Images**: attach or paste images (and text files). Only PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP are sent as images. Claude Code and Codex take them natively; Claude Code gets a text file (up to 1 MB) as a plain-text document, Codex gets its path; any other file (SVG, binaries, images over Claude's 5 MB limit) goes by path, with a notice. An ACP Agent (Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Devin CLI, dsh) gets image blocks when its ACP `initialize` advertises `promptCapabilities.image`; otherwise it gets each image's file path (as text and a `resource_link`), so it can open it with its file tools, and the timeline says it can't see the image itself. The composer says so before you send once the Agent has been asked. dsh answers `initialize` for the route its ACP starts on (its `acp` config row, which ships as a model dsh's catalog doesn't have) and refuses image blocks otherwise, so Agent Console starts dsh with a `--patch` overlay that puts that row on the conversation's model: on a model that sees images (Magpie writes those as `input: [text, image]`) dsh then takes image blocks; after a switch to another model in the same chat, images go by path and dsh opens them with its `read_image` tool. Checked on 2026-10-31 with the real CLIs, a throwaway HOME, no sign-in and a local stand-in for the model API (`npm run test:real`, see `test/real/`): the image reaches the model request from Claude Code 2.1.316 (stream-json), Codex 0.165.0, Copilot 1.0.105 (BYOK), OpenCode 1.19.5, Pi (pi-acp 0.0.34 + pi 1.4.0) and dsh 0.2.1-rc.5; Devin CLI 3000.11.234 and Cursor 2026.10.22 advertise images and Devin gets the image block, but both need a sign-in to run a model. Inline media is capped at 10 MB per file and 16 MB per message (an ACP SDK peer refuses messages over 32 MB); larger images go by path
- **Import history**: import matching sessions from `~/.claude/projects` and `~/.codex/sessions` as new threads (resumable)
- **Thread management**: search (Ctrl+K), pin, rename, archive, delete (trash), export Markdown, thread info (usage / cost / session ID)
- **Mock Agent**: `AGENT_CONSOLE_MOCK=1` registers a demo Agent with 8 scripts (`default` / `perm` / `plan` / `ask` / `slow` / `error` / `long` / `exit`) so UI work does not burn tokens

## Architecture

```
Magpie window
 └─ page/index.html  (sandbox="allow-scripts" iframe, served by Magpie from /_magpie/plugin/<per-run id>/)
     │ reads page/session.js  {port, key}  (gate key only, written by the plugin host)
     │ navigates itself to  http://127.0.0.1:<port>/open?k=<key>&theme=…
     ▼
Magpie plugin host (Bun) ── index.mjs + lib/gate.mjs  "gate" on 127.0.0.1:<port> (default 3488)
     │ first /open: spawns the daemon as a child process (node, --port 0, stdin lifeline, --parent-pid)
     │ 302 → http://127.0.0.1:<daemonPort>/?theme=…#t=<token>
     ▼
daemon (Node, daemon/dist/main.js) ── HTTP + WebSocket on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port
     └─ React app (app/) reads the token from location.hash, sends it as the x-agent-console header
        and in the WebSocket hello
```

## Security model

The daemon can run Agents with full access to your machine, so the token that unlocks it must never be readable by another web page.

- **Two secrets per plugin-host run.** Each run generates two independent random 256-bit values: a **gate key** and the **daemon token**. Only the gate key is ever written to a file.
- **Why `session.js` holds only the gate key.** Magpie serves the page folder at `/_magpie/plugin/<per-run id>/`, where the id is an HMAC that changes every time Magpie starts and is handed out only to Magpie's own window. Magpie does not check `Origin`, `Host`, `Sec-Fetch-*` or a cookie on these files, and sends no `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy`, so the unguessable path is their only protection. A classic `<script src>` include is not subject to CORS, so any page that learned the path (a different localhost port, a `file:` page, any website) could run `session.js` and read `globalThis.AgentConsoleSession`. That is why the file never contains the daemon token.
- **Token handoff.** After the gate binds its port, the host writes `{port, key}` to `page/session.js` (atomic write, mode 0600; git-ignored and excluded from the npm package). The page navigates to the gate's `/open?k=<key>`; the gate compares the key in constant time, starts or reuses the daemon and redirects to it with the daemon token **only in the URL fragment** (`#t=…`). The fragment is never sent to a server, written to a log, or leaked through `Referer`, and the window that ends up holding it belongs to the daemon's origin (an opaque origin inside Magpie's sandboxed frame), so the page that started the navigation cannot read it. A leaked gate key therefore lets another page at most open the console UI in a frame or tab it cannot read; it does not unlock the daemon's API or WebSocket. No HTML served by the daemon contains the token; an unauthenticated `GET /` returns a page with no secret in it.
- **`Origin: null` is not trusted.** Any site can produce `Origin: null` (sandboxed iframes, `data:` and `file:` pages). The token is the only authority:
  - static routes (`/`, `app.js`, …) refuse `Origin: null` and foreign origins with 403 and never send CORS headers;
  - token routes (`/api/*`, `/attachments/*`, WebSocket hello) accept `Origin: null` only as a way to *present* the token (the Magpie iframe has an opaque origin); `access-control-allow-origin: null` is emitted only on responses to requests that carried a valid token, plus the preflight for `/api/upload`; credentials are never allowed;
  - any other origin gets 403 even with a valid token.
- **Host is checked on every request and WebSocket upgrade** (gate and daemon): it must be `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` with the actually bound port, otherwise 421. This blocks DNS rebinding, where the attacker's requests carry no `Origin` at all.
- The gate answers only `GET /open?k=<gate key>` (the daemon token is not accepted there), refuses any request that carries an `Origin` header, and sends `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- WebSocket connections must send `hello` with the token within 5 seconds, otherwise they are closed with code 4401.

## Lifecycle

- Importing `index.mjs` has no side effects (no port, no process, no files).
- `server()` (called by Magpie's plugin host at host start-up — this includes short-lived hosts started by CLI commands such as `magpie plugin add` or `magpie plugin list`) binds the gate and writes `page/session.js`. If the port is busy it retries every 2 s in the background without blocking the host; a detached 0.1.0 daemon still holding the port is shut down once, only after it proves its identity by answering `/api/ping` with the token from `daemon.json`.
- The daemon starts when the page is opened for the first time and is reused for later opens. It is a normal (non-detached) child of the plugin host.
- The daemon exits when its stdin pipe closes or its parent pid disappears (checked every 2 s) — i.e. when Magpie quits or the plugin host restarts — and after 60 minutes idle.
- Magpie's plugin host treats the value returned by `server()` as OpenCode hooks and never calls `stop()`; it exits the Bun process when Magpie closes its stdin. A synchronous `exit` handler therefore closes the daemon's lifeline, signals it, and removes the `session.js` this host wrote. `stop()` (used by tests and other hosts) closes the gate, ends the daemon (graceful, then forced) and removes `session.js`.
- Agents stop with the daemon. Threads are persisted and can be resumed after reopening the page. On macOS/Linux every Agent CLI, the Codex app-server and the no-PTY shell run in their own process group, so stopping one ends everything it started; on Windows the same is done with `taskkill /T`. A process `exit` hook reaps any tree still alive when the daemon exits.

## Platforms

The plugin runs wherever Magpie runs (Windows, macOS, Linux). It needs **Node.js 20+** on `PATH`: Magpie's plugin host is Bun, but the daemon and `node-pty` need Node. If Node is missing, opening the page shows "Node.js was not found" (the gate's 503 page) instead of silently running under Bun; a too-old Node gives a similar message.

- **Finding Agent CLIs.** `PATH` is scanned in JavaScript (no `where.exe`/`which`; `where.exe` prints in the console code page, which garbled Chinese user names). The first hit in `PATH` order wins. Common install dirs are also searched because a GUI app may start with a minimal `PATH` (Magpie adds the login-shell `PATH` itself; this is a fallback): Homebrew (`/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`), `~/.local/bin`, npm global, Volta, Bun, `~/.claude/local`, `%APPDATA%\npm`.
- **Windows shims.** `.exe` runs directly; npm `.cmd` shims run their `cli.js` with Node; `.ps1`-only shims run with `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File`; any other `.cmd`/`.bat` runs through `cmd.exe` with cross-spawn-style escaping (spaces, `&`, `%`, quotes and Chinese in paths and arguments are safe).
- **Terminal.** `node-pty` prebuilds cover win32/darwin/linux × x64/arm64 (Linux prebuilds are glibc only). Default shell: Windows `pwsh` → `powershell` → `cmd`; macOS/Linux `$SHELL` if it exists, else `zsh` (macOS) / `bash` / `sh`. If `node-pty` cannot load, a simple non-PTY terminal is used ([details](#when-node-pty-cant-be-loaded)). On macOS the exec bit of `node-pty`'s `spawn-helper` is restored if the package extraction dropped it.
- **Folder picker.** Windows: PowerShell `FolderBrowserDialog`; macOS: `osascript` "choose folder"; Linux: `zenity` or `kdialog` when a graphical session exists; otherwise type the path.
- **Paths.** Project paths are compared case-insensitively on Windows and macOS (and NFC-normalized on macOS); `realpath.native` resolves 8.3 short names and `subst` drives; UNC paths work. Discarding an untracked file moves it to the trash with a copy fallback when the project and data dir are on different drives.
- **Encoding.** Agent output is decoded as UTF-8; the folder picker falls back to GBK (CP936); the file preview tries UTF-8, then GBK. Git runs with `core.quotepath=false` so Chinese file names show as-is.
- **Magpie desktop window → `http://127.0.0.1`.** Magpie's window origin is `wails://` on macOS/Linux and `http://wails.localhost` on Windows. The plugin frame navigates itself to the gate on `http://127.0.0.1`, as Magpie's plugin-runtime docs describe for page plugins. On macOS, Magpie's `Info.plist` has no ATS keys and ATS exempts IP-address hosts by default, and the main window has no CSP that could block the frame, so the navigation is allowed. This is the one item that still needs a run on a real Mac.
- **Clickjacking / `frame-ancestors`.** Not set on purpose. The UI must load inside Magpie's frame on every mode: `wails://` (a non-special scheme whose origin WebKit may treat as opaque), `http://wails.localhost`, and `magpie web` on any address, LAN IP or reverse proxy. No `frame-ancestors` list covers all of them without breaking one. Framing the console also requires the gate key, which only Magpie's per-run page path hands out.

## Reproducible build

`app/app.js`, `app/app.css`, `app/index.html`, `daemon/dist/main.js` and `daemon/dist/main.js.map` are committed build outputs of `web/src` and `daemon/src` (esbuild, options in `scripts/build-v1.mjs`). They are committed because this repository ships packages as they are checked in: `publish.yml` packs each package onto the `dist` branch with `npm pack --ignore-scripts` (`scripts/dist.mjs`) and publishes it with `npm publish` from its folder, with no install or build step. So the bundles in a pull request are exactly what users get, and `verify:build` proves they are the build of the source next to them.

The build is deterministic: no timestamps, no absolute paths, LF line endings enforced by `.gitattributes`. From this folder (`packages/agent-console`):

```bash
npm ci --workspaces=false              # the repository root is an npm workspace; this installs here, from this folder's package-lock.json
npm run build
git diff --exit-code app daemon/dist   # no output = identical bytes
npm run verify:build                   # rebuilds into a temp dir, byte-compares, prints SHA-256
```

`verify:build` prints `OK <sha256>  <file>` for each bundle and exits non-zero on any mismatch. Without `--workspaces=false`, npm treats this folder as a member of the root workspace and looks for a lockfile at the repository root, which there isn't.

## Dependencies

All dependencies and devDependencies are pinned to exact versions, and `package-lock.json` matches them (`npm ci` succeeds).

- **Installed for users** (`dependencies`): `@agentclientprotocol/sdk`, `ignore`, `ws`, `zod`. These are what `daemon/dist/main.js` imports (esbuild bundles it with `packages: "external"`, so every package it imports is loaded from `node_modules`); `index.mjs` itself only imports `ws`.
- **Optional** (`optionalDependencies`): `node-pty`, for the terminal panel only (see below).
- **Build only** (`devDependencies`): the UI packages `react`, `react-dom`, `@xterm/xterm`, `@xterm/addon-fit`, `lucide-react`, `marked`, `dompurify`, `highlight.js`, `zustand`, `@tanstack/react-virtual` and `clsx` are bundled into `app/app.js` and never loaded from `node_modules` at run time, plus esbuild, TypeScript, vitest and type packages.
- No Claude Code or Anthropic package is installed or bundled: the Claude Code Agent is the user's own `claude` CLI, started per conversation and driven over its stream-json protocol (`daemon/src/providers/claude/cli.ts`).

### Why `node-pty` is `1.2.0-beta.15`

Magpie installs a plugin with `bun add` and does not run its dependencies' install scripts (usemagpie.ai/docs/plugins, "Installing"). `node-pty`'s own `install` script (`node scripts/prebuild.js || node-gyp rebuild`) therefore never runs, so the only binary a user gets is the one inside `node-pty`'s npm tarball under `prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/`.

- `node-pty@1.1.0`, the current `latest`, ships prebuilds for `darwin-x64`, `darwin-arm64`, `win32-x64` and `win32-arm64` only. On Linux it has no binary at all unless `node-gyp` compiles one at install time, which Magpie never does.
- `node-pty@1.2.0-beta.2` and later add `linux-x64` and `linux-arm64` prebuilds (glibc 2.28 or newer). `1.2.0-beta.15` is the beta this plugin is built and tested against, pinned exactly so a later, untested beta is never picked up (`beta.16`–`beta.18` came out on 2026-10-22/23). It also drops winpty, which more than halves the tarball (27 MB unpacked, against 64 MB for 1.1.0).
- The prebuilds are N-API addons, so one binary works on every Node version from 20 up; Node upgrades need no rebuild.

Checked with `npm view node-pty versions dist-tags` and by listing `prebuilds/` in the `1.1.0`, `1.2.0-beta.1` … `beta.15` tarballs. Once a stable `node-pty` release ships the Linux prebuilds, the pin moves to it.

### When `node-pty` can't be loaded

Only the terminal panel is affected; the daemon, the Agents and everything else keep working.

- No prebuild for the machine (for example Linux on musl/Alpine, 32-bit ARM, or glibc older than 2.28), a binary that fails to load, or `node-pty` missing because an install that does run scripts failed to build it: `node-pty` is loaded lazily, only when a terminal is opened, and the load error is caught and logged (`node-pty 加载失败，终端退化无 PTY 方案` in `logs/`).
- `pty.spawn` throwing (for example macOS `posix_spawnp failed`) is caught the same way. On macOS the exec bit of `spawn-helper` is restored first, since some extractions drop it.
- In both cases the terminal opens as a plain shell over pipes, and the panel shows "Simple terminal (no full TTY programs)". Commands run and print, but full-screen programs (vim, top, less) and line editing need a real TTY and don't work there.
- `node-pty` is an `optionalDependency`, so an `npm install` that runs install scripts and can't build it still installs the plugin.

`test/v1/terminal-fallback.test.ts` covers both cases: `node-pty` failing to import and `pty.spawn` throwing.

## Data directory

```
$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/magpie/agent-console/   (default ~/.config/magpie/agent-console on every OS;
                                           on Windows ~ is %USERPROFILE%, the same root Magpie uses)
  daemon.json          pid/port/token/version of the running daemon (mode 0600)
  settings.json        settings (default Agent / permission / send key / panel widths…)
  projects.json        project list
  threads/<id>/        meta.json + timeline.jsonl (event persistence, replay on reconnect)
  attachments/         uploaded files
  trash/               deleted threads and discarded new files (not hard-deleted)
  logs/                daily rotating logs (kept 7 days); logs/daemon-spawn.log has the plugin host's view
```

Magpie in portable mode keeps its own config next to the executable, but this plugin still uses the directory above (it follows `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`).

## Development

In `packages/agent-console`, after `npm ci --workspaces=false` (use `npm install --workspaces=false` too when changing dependencies, so the lockfile stays in this folder):

```bash
npm run build      # daemon esm + web iife (app/ and daemon/dist are committed)
npm run verify:build  # check committed bundles match a clean build
npm run dev        # daemon on port 3499, data dir _tmp/xdg-dev (does not touch real data)
npm run check      # typecheck both tsconfigs
npm test           # vitest (test/v1 + web/src); the repository's root `bun test` skips these (bunfig.toml) and runs agent-console.test.mjs
npm run e2e:v1     # e2e: spawn daemon(3497) + Edge/Chrome/Chromium, Mock Agent (MSEDGE_PATH / CHROME_PATH to override)
node scripts/verify-windows.mjs [--quick]   # one-command platform self-check, see docs/VERIFY-windows.md
npm run shot:v1    # screenshot set (light/dark × scenes → _tmp/shots-v1/)

# Mock (no real tokens)
AGENT_CONSOLE_MOCK=1 npm run dev
# scripts: default /perm /plan /ask /slow /error /long (5000-event stress) /exit
```

| Env | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `AGENT_CONSOLE_PORT` | gate port in the plugin / daemon port in standalone mode (3488; plugin `options.port` wins) |
| `AGENT_CONSOLE_MOCK=1` | register the mock provider |
| `AGENT_CONSOLE_TOKEN` | fixed page token (tests/screenshots only; do not set in production) |
| `AGENT_CONSOLE_IDLE_EXIT_MIN` | idle auto-exit minutes (default 60) |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | data root (`_tmp/xdg-dev` in development) |

Daemon CLI: `node daemon/dist/main.js [--port N|0] [--data DIR] [--token T] [--parent-pid PID]`. In standalone mode (no `--parent-pid`) it prints the URL to open, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/#t=<token>`, to the console.

## License

MIT (see LICENSE). Third-party licenses are in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md: the 5 installed packages and the 11 bundled into `app/app.js` (mostly MIT; DOMPurify MPL-2.0/Apache-2.0, highlight.js BSD-3-Clause, lucide-react ISC). Build/test: esbuild, vitest, TypeScript, playwright-core.

Architecture takes cues from Paseo (persistent daemon + provider abstraction) and T3 Code (timeline shape and three-column layout) — ideas only, no copied code.
